en: Oṃ, homage to the Buddha!
The Epic Poem *Saundarananda*,
Canto One: A Description of Kapilavastu.
There was a sage named Kapila Gautama, the best among the upholders of dharma, who,
like Gautama Kākṣīvat, had grown weary from his ascetic penances.
He who constantly resorted to radiant asceticism like Kāśyapa, and attained supreme perfection in its increase like Kāśyapa. (Saundarananda 1.2)
He who, like Vasiṣṭha, milked the cow for his own sake from the sacrificial oblations, and like Vasiṣṭha, milked the cow from his disciples who were perfected by austerity. (Saundarananda 1.3)
By virtue of his great majesty and long asceticism, he was like a second [Dīrghatapas],
and by his wisdom, he was like a third [son] of Kāvya and Aṅgiras.
On the auspicious side of that vast Himavat mountain,
there was a field and a sanctuary, which became an hermitage for his austerities.
With its beautiful groves of trees and thickets, and its lush, soft,
green meadows, it always appeared like a cloud due to the canopy of sacrificial smoke.
With its soft, smooth, and pale-yellow sand dunes,
and its uncluttered stretches of ground, the place appeared as if it were adorned with cosmetic ointments.
It stood as if possessed of kinsmen in the form of lakes filled with lotuses— lakes that were pure, reckoned as sacred fords, purifying, and inspiring.
With forest groves on all sides filled with fully developed fruits and flowers,
Nara shone and flourished like a man possessed of effective means.
Though crowded with ascetics contented with wild rice and fruits, self-composed, peaceful, and free from worldly desire, it seemed utterly empty.
There, the sound was heard of fires being offered oblations,
of crested peacocks crying out, and of sacred bathing places during their ritual ablutions.
There, the deer, sleeping upon the pure sacrificial altars,
shone as if they were offerings made with *mādhavī* flowers and parched grain.
Even the small animals wandered there peacefully with the deer,
as if they had learned discipline from the ascetics who provide refuge.
Even though rebirth was still uncertain and the scriptures were contradictory,
those whose wealth is austerity practiced penance there as if they were perceiving it directly before their eyes.
In this place, the Brahman is measured by some, yet by others it is not measured;
Soma is measured at the proper time, but never is he measured at an improper time.
Indifferent toward their bodies, those ascetics, whose own intellects were fixed on the Dharma,
practiced austerities with great effort as if they were filled with joy.
There, sages striving with minds intent on attaining heaven seemed,
through their passion for austerity, to bring about the very destruction of dharma.
Then certain princes of the Ikṣvāku lineage, desiring to dwell there, went to that hermitage, the abode of splendor and field of asceticism.
With bodies like golden pillars, lion-like chests, and mighty arms,
they were the worthy recipients of great renown, prosperity, and humility.
For those of noble form are indeed unsuited to one who is unworthy, the high-souled to one of fickle mind, and the wise to a younger brother who is devoid of wisdom. 1.20.
They endured the royal splendor that had come to them as their mother’s dowry,
and they protected their father’s truth, which was why they retired to the forest.
The sage Kapila Gautama became their preceptor;
thus, because of their teacher’s lineage, those who were Kautsas became Gautamas.
Just as two brothers who share the same father become distinct through their separate acceptance of teachers—
one was Rāma Gārgya and the other was Vāsudeva Gautama.
And because they made their dwelling concealed by śāka trees,
therefore those of the Ikṣvāku lineage are known on earth as Śākyas.
Gautama performed for them rites befitting his own lineage,
just as the sage Bhārgava did for the prince Sagara.
Kaṇva was like [the father] of the energetic Bharata, son of Śakuntalā;
and the wise Vālmīki was like [the father] of the two wise sons of Maithilī.
That forest, by means of that sage and those preeminent kṣatriyas,
simultaneously bore the splendor of both the Brahmanical and the Kṣatriya orders— peaceful and well-guarded.
Then, taking up a water-pitcher with the desire to ensure their prosperity,
that sage flew up into the sky and spoke to those princes.
"Let the stream that falls from this jar of inexhaustible water reach me in due order, without overstepping it. (Saundarananda 1.29)
Then, having said "So be it," and having prostrated with their heads,
they all mounted their well-adorned chariots drawn by swift horses.
Then, followed by them as they stood upon their chariots,
he traversed the sky and sprinkled water over the edge of that hermitage’s grounds.
Having drawn a checkerboard pattern as it were with auspicious signs that made the ground fragrant, the sage stood there and spoke thus to the daughters of the king: *Saundarananda 1.32*
"When I have departed for the celestial realm, you must construct a city within this area defined by the moat and marked by the sign of the rim. (Saundarananda 1.33)
Then, on one occasion, when that sage had departed, those heroes, unrestrained by youth, roamed about like elephants without a goad. (Saundarananda 1.34)
With finger-guards of iguana-skin bound on their hands, bows held in their grasp,
great quivers filled with arrows, and their garments tightly fastened, they stood ready.
Seeking to test his skill among both serpents and wild beasts,
they imitated the forest-dwelling son of Duṣyanta, Devakarmā.
Seeing them returned to their natural state like aged tiger cubs,
the ascetics abandoned that forest and took refuge in the Himalayas.
Then, seeing that hermitage site empty of them, those whose minds were desolate, tormented by grief, sighed like venomous serpents. (Saundarananda 1.38)
Then those performers of meritorious deeds, whose prosperity was manifest,
obtained great treasures described there by those who know them.
Enough with the pursuit of all the aims of dharma, artha, and kāma;
you possess many various kinds of treasures that are free from enemies.
Then, because of the acquisition of that site and due to the transformation of their past karma,
those who were skilled in architecture established a magnificent city upon that ground.
With moats as wide as rivers, clearly defined and winding great highways,
and massive ramparts resembling mountains, it was like another Giri-vraja.
With its white palaces as its beautiful face and its well-arranged market-stalls,
it was surrounded by rows of mansions like the central valley of the Himalayas.
There, the Brahmins— learned in the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, established in the six duties—
chanted the sacred hymns for the sake of peace and prosperity.
In that land, by his own power, he caused the punishments for servants to be proclaimed so as to turn back those who would attack his territory.
In that place, they stationed as overseers those who were endowed with the wealth of virtuous conduct, possessed of modesty and foresight,
worthy, heroic, skillful, and heads of households.
He appointed those ministers to various corresponding duties, each endowed with specific qualities such as intelligence, eloquence, and prowess.
Crowded with men who were wealthy, composed, highly learned, and free from pride, it shone like Mount Mandara filled with Kinnaras.
There, with joyful minds and desiring to please the citizens,
they constructed magnificent dwellings known as pleasure gardens, which were abodes of glory.
And by his command, out of an excellence of consciousness, auspicious lotus-pools with water of the highest and most sublime quality were dug in all directions.
They established throughout the surroundings charming, magnificent, and excellent assembly halls, complete with wells, along the roads and in the groves.
Crowded with elephants, horses, and chariots, yet not congested and free from turmoil;
where the wealth of supplicants was never hidden, while his own wisdom and prowess remained concealed.
Like a repository for riches, like a source of splendors,
like a home for sciences, and like a meeting place for all prosperities.
He was a wish-granting tree for the virtuous, a refuge for those seeking shelter,
a source of delight for those versed in the scriptures, and a tethering post for those endowed with great strength of arm.
With assemblies, festivals, gifts, and ritual observances, those heroes of immense prowess adorned that city, the abode of the world. (Saundarananda 1.55)
Because they did not impose any unjust tax upon anyone,
they filled that city with prosperity in a very short time.
And because they built that city on the site of the hermitage belonging to that seer Kapila, it was therefore called Kapilavastu.
Just as cities are heard of in the hermitages of Kakanda, Makanda, and Kuśāmba, so too was that [city] of Kapila. 1.58.
Those sons, resembling Indra in their splendor, entered that city not out of pride but through their noble majesty;
and from that time on, they were ever-famed for the fragrance of their glory, just like the sons of Yayāti.
Even though it was governed by princes who were themselves its lords, the kingdom did not shine while it remained without a king;
it was like the sky when the moon has not yet risen, despite being illuminated by thousands of stars.
He who was the eldest among those brothers in years and in virtues, a bull among bulls in his vigor—
those who held their guru dear consecrated him there, as the Ādityas consecrated the thousand-eyed Indra in heaven.

Possessed of right conduct, discipline, policy, and ritual action, he protected the kingdom for the sake of dharma and not for the pleasure of the senses; holding the royal parasol, surrounded by his brothers, he was like Indra followed by the Maruts as he protects heaven.
The first canto, titled "Description of Kapilavastu," in the epic poem *Saundarananda*, is concluded.
The second canto: King Śuddhodana.
Then, after some time, by virtue of his lineage,
there arose a king named Śuddhodana, whose actions were pure and who had conquered his senses.
He who did not cling to sensual pleasures, nor was he amazed by the attainment of prosperity;
he did not despise others for their success, nor was he distressed because of others.
He was powerful, endowed with courage, learned, and wise;
he was valiant, possessed of statesmanship, steadfast, and of pleasant countenance.
He was handsome yet not arrogant, skillful yet not lacking in uprightness; he was radiant yet patient, and an active doer yet free from self-conceit.
Though assailed by enemies in battle and sought for refuge by his friends,
he never turned his face away, owing to his splendor and his very desire to give.
Desiring to follow the path of righteousness traversed by former kings,
he emulated his ancestors in conduct, carrying the burden of the kingdom as if it were a sacred initiation.
Through his excellent administration and protection, the subjects lived in happiness, free from anxiety, as if resting upon the lap of a father. (Saundarananda 2.7)
Whether he had mastered the scriptures or the arts of weaponry, or whether he was born into a noble family,
no one who came into his presence failed to see that his purpose remained unfulfilled.
Though addressed with words that were beneficial yet unpleasant, he listened well and was not disturbed;
having abandoned even much evil, he remembered even the smallest good deed.
He showed favor to those who bowed before him; he subdued his enemies;
he protected those in distress; and he chastised those who did not remain on the path.
For the most part, those who followed his character were seen acquiring virtues just as they acquired wealth within that sphere of influence.
He studied the supreme Brahman and never wavered from steadfastness;
he bestowed gifts upon worthy recipients and committed no sin whatsoever. (Saundarananda 2.12)
With fortitude, he upheld his vow like a noble steed bearing its yoke;
for once fallen from truth, he did not desire life even for a moment.
He attended upon the learned, shone forth through his self-possession,
and gleamed before the disciplined like the moon in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa.
Through both his intellect and his study of the scriptures, he understood what was appropriate for this world and the next;
and through both his fortitude and his prowess, he protected both his senses and his subjects.
He took away the suffering of the afflicted and the exalted glory of his enemies; and by means of his policies, he acquired both the earth and even greater fame.
By nature compassionate, he felt sorrow upon seeing those who were suffering;
nor did he, out of greed for fame, acquire wealth through unjust means.
Because of his firm devotion born of friendship, even toward friends who were devoid of merit,
he did not fail to give each person their respective wealth out of a cheerful disposition.
Without having first offered the best portion to the Arhats, he did not eat anything;
nor did he milk the cow by unrighteous means, as one might do out of a thirst for milk.
He did not consume offerings that had not been brought to him, nor did he ascend to the heights of pride or lordship;
he sharpened his intellect through the scriptures for the sake of Dharma, and not for the sake of fame.
Yet he did not afflict even those who were worthy of his affliction with defiled actions;
and because of his noble nature, he did not overlook the virtues even of his enemies.
Like the moon, he drew the eyes of the people toward him with his physical form;
yet he did not covet another's property on earth, as one would avoid a highly venomous serpent.
In his realm, no one was ever harmed by anyone anywhere;
for he commanded that the bow held in his hand grant fearlessness to those in distress.
He looked upon even those who had committed offenses with a moist glance, let alone those who had previously done him kindness; he refreshed them with gentle words.
He acquired many branches of knowledge, yet remained free from curiosity regarding sense-objects;
established in the dharma of the Kṛta age, he did not falter from righteousness even in times of hardship.
He constantly increased in virtues, grew through the excellence of his friends, remained steadfast among the elders, and did not turn toward a censurable path. (Saundarananda 2.26)
With his arrows he quelled his enemies; with his virtues he delighted his kinsmen;
with his faults he did not incite his servants; and with his taxes he did not oppress his subjects. (Saundarananda 2.27)
Through protection and through valor, he sowed the entire earth;
and by means of clear penal law, he caused the night-sacrifices to flourish.
By the conduct of a royal seer, he caused the fragrance of fame to spread through his lineage;
with his brilliance, he dispelled darkness, just as the sun dispels it with its splendor.
He caused his ancestors to expand through virtues equal to those of a worthy son,
and he gladdened the subjects with his conduct, just as a rain cloud refreshes them with water.
Through his constant and abundant gifts, he caused the Soma plant to flourish for the Brahmins;
and by abiding by the duties of kingship, he caused the crops to ripen in due season.
Free from doubt, he did not engage in unrighteous discourse;
like a universal monarch, he subdued his enemies for the sake of Dharma.
He did not diminish the kingdom or the army in any way;
rather, through his servants alone, he vigorously shattered the pride of his enemies.
By his own virtues alone, he caused his lineage to flourish ever more and more;
yet, through the established order of all dharmas, he never caused his subjects to suffer.
Unwearied, the performer of sacrifices measured out the sacrificial ground at the proper time;
and by protecting the twice-born, he caused the Veda to flourish without anxiety.
At the proper time, he respectfully caused the moon to swell according to the injunctions of his gurus;
by means of his austerity and splendor, he caused the army of his enemies to wither away.
The knower of the supreme dharma caused his subjects to dwell in subtle righteousness;
and by the very vision of that dharma, he caused them to dwell in heaven at the proper time.
Even though he was clearly visible, he did not appoint one who was unrighteous to difficult tasks;
nor, out of mere affection, did he promote one who was incompetent due to passion.
With his splendor and radiance, he caused his arrogant enemies to tremble;
and with his blazing lamp of fame, he caused the entire earth to tremble.
Out of consideration for its benefit and not for the sake of fame, he gave that great wealth to the seeker; yet, having renounced even such vast property, he incurred no infamy whatsoever.
Therefore, even an enemy afflicted by suffering was not abandoned when he sought refuge;
nor did he feel pride after conquering even arrogant foes. (Saundarananda 2.41)
He did not transgress the bounds of propriety out of desire, hatred, or even fear;
thus, although enjoyments were present, he did not indulge in the habitual functioning of the senses.
By him no difficult task whatsoever was ever seen as impossible;
in the performance of what is unpleasant or pleasant, he never became inactive.
Accordingly, he drank the Soma and acquired fame as was fitting for his kalpa;
he constantly studied the Vedas and practiced the dharma prescribed by the Vedas.
Thus, through such qualities that were difficult to find, that Śākya king— though surrounded by vassal lords who were themselves powerful— became as invincible as Śakra.
Then, at that time, the gods, desiring the Dharma and wishing to behold the practice of righteousness, wandered through the various quarters of the world.
Wandering through the world with a desire to investigate dharma, those whose souls were devoted to dharma beheld that king, who was preeminently a soul devoted to dharma.
Then, descending from the Tuṣita gods to the earth, the Bodhisattva made his vow for rebirth in the family of that lord of the earth.
At that time, the queen of that god among men was named Māyā;
she was free from anger, darkness, and illusion, like the goddess Māyā in heaven.
Then, at that time, she saw in a dream a white six-tusked elephant entering her womb, possessing a splendor like that of Airāvata. (Saundarananda 2.50)
Having heard that dream, the twice-born experts in dreams interpreted it as foretelling the birth of a prince who would be the bearer of fortune, virtue, and glory.
When that distinguished being was born— one who seeks the destruction of birth—
the earth, though normally immovable, trembled like a ship struck by waves.
An unblemished rain of flowers fell from the sky through the rays of the sun,
as if shaken from the Caitraratha grove by the trunks of the elephants of the quarters.
In the sky, the drums resounded like those of the sporting Maruts;
the sun shone with exceeding brilliance, and an auspicious breeze blew. (Saundarananda 2.54)
The Tuṣita and Śuddhāvāsa deities were indeed filled with joy,
out of great reverence for the True Dharma and out of compassion for sentient beings.
The supreme one, who brings about the banner of welfare, approached Yaśaḥketu;
he shone with peaceful splendor like Dharma incarnate.
To the younger queen, Araṇyā, as fire is born in the forest, a son named Nanda was born, who brought constant joy to the family. (Saundarananda 2.57)
Long-armed, broad-chested, with shoulders like a lion’s and eyes like a bull’s,
he who by his preeminent form truly bore the epithet "Sundara" (the Handsome One).
Like the month of Madhu arrived, like the moon newly risen,
and like the bodiless Love-god endowed with limbs, he shone with lovely splendor.
The lord of men caused those two to grow with supreme joy,
just as great wealth held in the hands of a virtuous person causes both dharma and kama to flourish.
In time, two noble sons grew up for his welfare,
just as Dharma and Artha arise for the prosperity of a noble man who has undertaken great endeavors.
Between those two excellent sons, that King of the Śākyas shone resplendent,
like the Middle Country clearly situated between the Himavat and Pāriyātra mountains.
Then, after those two sons of the king had been consecrated and had gradually mastered their learning,
Nanda took constant delight in sensual pleasures, but Sarvārthasiddha did not find pleasure in them.
Having beheld the aged, the afflicted, and the dead, and reflecting upon the world’s ignorance, his heart was filled with distress;
with a compassion deeply rooted in his soul and desiring to utterly destroy the fear of birth and death on all sides, he no longer found delight in the objects of the senses.
Out of world-weariness, having fixed his mind on the state of no-return,
he departed from the royal palace at night— indifferent to the sleeping women and intent on going to the forest— like a swan leaving a lake where the lotuses have been crushed.
The second canto, titled "Description of the King," in the epic poem *Saundarananda* is completed.
The third canto: "Description of the Tathāgata."

Then, having abandoned Kapilavastu—crowded with throngs of horses, elephants, and chariots, magnificent and inhabited by people devoted to him out of fearlessness—he went to the forest with a resolute mind for the sake of asceticism. *Saundarananda 3.1*
Having observed those sages engaged in various ascetic practices and relying on diverse rules of discipline,
he turned away from such unstable austerity, seeing them to be wretched through their thirst for sense-objects.

Then, having attended upon Ārāḍa, who taught liberation, as well as Udraka, whose mind was set on tranquility, he—whose intellect was fixed on reality and who was skilled in the paths—declared: "I too have abandoned this which is not the path."
Reflecting upon what might be supreme in the world, he studied various scriptures;
yet, failing to attain certainty, he practiced even more difficult austerities under another teacher.
Then, perceiving that "this is not the path," he abandoned even that extensive austerity;
having understood the supreme object of meditation, he partook of excellent food for the sake of attaining immortality.
With arms as long and thick as golden yokes, with the gait of a bull and long eyes,
he approached a Plakṣa tree in order to understand the supreme method of ascetic discipline.
Having sat there with a resolute mind and unshakable fortitude like the king of mountains,
he then conquered the fierce army of Māra and awakened to the auspicious, unassailable, and imperishable state.
And having understood that he had accomplished his task, the gods, their minds set on immortality, attained a joy beyond compare;
yet the assembly of Māra, turning away from them, was agitated with grief.
The earth with its mountains trembled; Śiva, the friend of fire, blew [his conch];
the drums of the gods resounded; and the sky, though devoid of clouds, rained down.
And having realized the supreme, undecaying ultimate truth, the Lord, out of compassion,
went to the city surrounded by Varanasi in order to demonstrate the eternal immortality.

Then, for the welfare of the world, the Sage turned the Wheel of Dharma— whose hub is the Deathless, whose rim is steadfastness, intelligence, and concentration, and whose spokes are discipline and restraint— within that assembly.
"Thus, this is suffering; this is its proliferating creeper of origination;
this is peace; and this is the means"—this supreme tetrad is distinguished according to its specific parts. (Saundarananda 3.12)
And having proclaimed that peerless, supreme, and irreversible Dharma in its three turnings and twelve aspects, the Seer first instructed him whose lineage was Kauṇḍinya.

For he had crossed over, and caused the world to cross over as well, that fathomless ocean of faults, whose waters are the acquisitions (upadhi), which teems with creatures of mental affliction (ādhi), and which is stirred by the waves of anger, pride, and fear.
Having disciplined many people among the Kāśis and the Gayas, as well as in Girivraja,
that one of supreme compassion then went to his father’s city out of a desire to favor it.
For Gautama, whose body was like the sun, arose and dispelled the darkness— like the sun itself— for those people who were devoted to sense objects and followed many various paths.
Then, all around, he beheld Kapilavastu— renowned for its most auspicious foundations and its exceedingly pure and peaceful groves— with a lack of desire, as if it were a mere forest.

For he had become one who possessed nothing, his mind fixed and himself the master of his own soul; how much less, then, could he have attachment for kinsmen, people of his own country, friends, or material things—all of which produce manifold fears? (Saundarananda 3.18)

He did not rejoice at being honored, nor did he fall into grief through contempt; firm in his resolve, he underwent no change of state toward either the sword or sandalwood, nor toward suffering and pleasure.
Then the king, having learned that his son had approached the Tathāgata,
set out quickly with only a few horses following him, out of an eager longing to see his son.
The Sugata, beholding the Tathāgata and perceiving that the king was lacking in resolve,
flew up into the sky with the desire to lead even the rest of the people, whose faces were bathed in tears.
He strode across as if through heaven and earth; he sat down again after having stood;
with an unmoving mind, he lay down; he became manifold again, and likewise became one again. (Saundarananda 3.22)
He moved upon the water as if on land, and entered the earth as if it were water;
like a cloud he rained down repeatedly in the sky, and like the newly risen sun, he blazed forth.
Blazing simultaneously like a fire and emitting water like a cloud,
he shone with a luster resembling molten gold, like a cloud illuminated by the twilight.
Beholding that banner, which rose up as if encircled by a net of gold and jewels,
the king attained incomparable joy, and the prostrate people offered him great respect.

Then, perceiving that the lord of men had been made a fit vessel by his wealth of supernatural power, and seeing that the citizens were likewise inclined toward him, the Guide proclaimed the Dharma and Discipline.
Then the king first obtained the fruit for the sake of accomplishing the dharma of immortality;
having attained incomparable dharma from the sage, he bowed to that sage as if to a guru.

Then many of the Śākya bulls, who were skillful, possessed serene minds, and were terrified by the suffering of birth and death, went forth like bulls fleeing from the fear of fire. (Saundarananda 3.28)

But even those who did not abandon their homes out of regard for their children, fathers, and mothers, they too undertook the rules of discipline until death and maintained them with concentrated minds. (Saundarananda 3.29)
He did not harm even the smallest creature, though he lived by the slaughter of others;
how much more so, then, one who was noble-born, possessed of vast virtues, ever compassionate, and devoted to the service of the Sage?

Though his efforts were undiminished and his wealth was meager, and though he could not endure the insults of others, he did not seize the riches of another; for he trembled before the power of another as if it were a venomous serpent.

Although he was endowed with wealth, though he was young, and though his senses were fickle toward sense-objects, he never approached the wives of others; for he considered them to be even more burning than fire itself.

No one spoke an untruth, nor did anyone utter even the truth if it were unpleasant; no one spoke even a gentle word that was not beneficial, and no one uttered even what was beneficial if it involved backbiting. (Saundarananda 3.33)
He was never mentally lured by the wealth of others, nor did his mind ever crave them;
reflecting upon sensual pleasure as being no true happiness, that virtuous man dwelt there as if already satisfied.
Moreover, being compassionate, he did not even think of causing harm to another;
for there, the people regarded one another as if they were their own mother, father, son, or friend.

He attained the correct vision that the fruit of karma will inevitably come to pass in the future, as well as in the present and the past; furthermore, he perceived that the destiny of beings in the world is likewise determined.
Thus, by means of these ten kinds of supreme, abundant, and virtuous actions,
the people there dwelt in reliance upon the Sage, even though the age was declining and its virtues were becoming lax.
And yet, because of those qualities, no one there desired the happiness of rebirth;
having understood all existence to be inauspicious, they turned toward the destruction of existence, not toward further birth. (Saundarananda 3.38)
Even householders, free from doubt and possessing supremely purified vision, entered the stream; indeed, many did so, while others even brought about the thinning of the dust of passion.

Even he who, in this world, indulged in sense-objects according to his means, remained devoted to renunciation, humility, and self-restraint; he too moved about without ever straying from the path of the righteous.
Moreover, there was no fear from oneself, nor from others, nor from fate;
and in that Kṛta age, the people rejoiced in the qualities of great happiness and abundance, as in the time of Manu.

Thus that city became joyful, free from affliction, and devoid of calamity— resembling the cities of the Kurus, the Raghus, and the Purus— while the Great Seer, the teacher of fearlessness, dwelt there for the sake of its welfare, having transcended all passion.
The third canto, titled "Description of the Tathāgata," in the epic poem *Saundarananda* is completed.
Canto Four: The Request for His Wife.
But even while the sage was speaking there of the Dharma, and while his kinsmen remained indifferent toward that Dharma,
Nanda— dwelling in the palace, devoted solely to the affairs of passion, and accompanied by his beloved— continued to enjoy himself.
For, united with his beloved as a ruddy goose is with its mate,
he who was worthy of love did not think of Vaiśravaṇa nor of Śakra for the sake of their realms, much less of the Dharma.
Because of her fortune and her beauty she was called "Sundarī" (the Beautiful); because of her steadfastness and her pride she was called "Māninī" (the Proud);
and because of her radiance and her dignity she was called "Bhāminī" (the Illustrious)—thus she was addressed by these three names.

That lotus-like woman shone even more brightly with the sun of her own lineage’s joy— the sun that was her smile for its swans, her eyes for its bees, and her full breasts for its lofty, upturned lotus buds.
With a form exceedingly captivating and with gestures corresponding to that form, she was indeed the Sundarī among women and Nanda among men in the world of mortals at that time. (Saundarananda 4.5)
That goddess was like one who wanders in the Nandana grove, and Nanda was the bringer of joy to his family;
they appeared as if created by the Sustainer of Beings, having surpassed mortals yet not having reached the status of gods.

If Nanda were not to obtain that Sundarī, or if she of the arched brows were not to attend upon him, that pair would surely not shine, being incomplete like the night and the moon deprived of one another. (Saundarananda 4.7)
Like the target of Love and Passion, like the nest of Joy and Ecstasy,
and like the vessel of Rapture and Contentment, he took as his wife that pair who were blinded by intoxication.
With eyes intent on gazing at one another, with minds attached to each other’s conversation,
and with the body-unguents removed by their mutual embrace— that couple captivated one another.
Both of them, impassioned by love and dwelling by a mountain torrent like a Kinnarī and a Kiṃpuruṣa,
played together and shone brightly, as if vying with one another in the splendor of their beauty.
By increasing their mutual passion, that couple took pleasure with one another;
in the intervals between exhaustion, by means of mutual diversion, they joyfully intoxicated one another with playful grace.
Then, desiring to serve his beloved, he adorned her, yet not for the sake of mere decoration;
for she, already adorned by her own natural beauty, was the ornament even of ornaments.
Then, placing a mirror in his hand, she said to her beloved, "Hold this for a moment before me while I apply my forehead mark"; and he held it for her. (Saundarananda 4.13)
Then, looking at her husband’s beard, she applied a tilaka mark upon it in that very same way;
and Nanda, having cured the mirror with the breath of his sighs, struck it down.
She laughed inwardly at her husband’s graceful gestures and his deceit;
and though she was indeed angry with him, she knit her brows in a frown upon her forehead. (Saundarananda 4.15)
With his left hand, languid with intoxication, he cast a *karṇotpala* flower upon his shoulder;
then, with its petals as fingers, he pressed that very same flower against his face, whose eyes were half-closed.
Then Nanda, out of fear, bowed his head at the feet of his beloved; those feet, which shone like lotuses, were adorned with moving anklets and had toes illuminated by the luster of her nails.

Then, with his head adorned by the blossoming flowers he had released, he who did what was pleasing to his beloved shone like a *nāga* tree on a golden altar, its branches bent by the wind as if weighed down by an excess of flowers.
With the string of her necklace displaced by her breasts, she raised him up, pressing him with both arms;
"How have you been made thus? she laughed aloud, her face turned sideways so that her earrings were askew.
Then, repeatedly looking at her husband’s face as his hand rested upon the mirror,
she completed that decorative mark on her cheek, which was moist with *tamāla* leaf-paste.
Her face, with its tamāla-leaf ornament, copper-red lower lip, and eyes as long as her hair,
shone like a lotus with its stalk still attached, its tips reddened by pollen, and bees alighting upon it.
Then Nanda, respectfully holding a mirror as a witness to his adornment,
with eyes squinting to inspect the decorative marks, gazed at the face of his beloved as she playfully flirted.
Beholding his beloved’s face— beautiful with its distinctive mark bitten by her earrings, like a lotus bruised by a *kāraṇḍava* duck— Nanda became once again the bringer of joy to his beloved.
In that celestial palace, within its inner chamber, Nanda rejoiced in that very manner;
and the Tathāgata, at the time when it was proper to go for alms, entered his house for the sake of alms.
With his face cast down and devoid of courtesy, he remained in his brother’s house just as if he were in the house of a stranger;
then, due to the negligence of the servants, he returned without having obtained even alms.
One woman ground fragrant unguents for the body, while another perfumed her garments;
another prepared the ritual for bathing, and others wove fragrant garlands.
In that house, while performing their graceful duties suited to play for their master, some young women did not perceive the Buddha; this was surely the intention of the Buddha.
But one woman, standing there upon the roof of the palace, having fixed her gaze through the lattice of a window,
beheld the Sugata emerging like the blazing sun from within the womb of a cloud.

Considering there the respect due to her husband and her own devotion toward the Arhat, she stood before Nanda, desiring to speak; and with his permission, she then related it thus: *Saundarananda 4.29*
I suspect that the Blessed One has entered our house as a teacher to show favor to these people;
for, having received neither alms, nor speech, nor a seat, he departs once more like from an empty wilderness.
Hearing that the great seer had entered his house and was departing again without receiving due honors, he—
adorned with variegated ornaments, garments, and garlands like a wish-fulfilling tree— trembled as if shaken by the wind.
Then, placing his lotus-like hands in añjali upon his head, he requested his beloved to go with him:
"I shall go to pay my respects to my teacher; you should grant me permission to depart."
Trembling, she embraced him like a creeper shaken by the wind;
with eyes rolling and bathed in tears, she sighed deeply and spoke these words.
"I ought not to cause you, who are desirous of going to see your teacher, any hindrance to your dharma.
Go, noble son, and return very quickly, before this cosmetic paste has dried."
If you were indeed to be procrastinating, I would inflict a great punishment upon you;
I would wake you repeatedly as you lay there with my breasts pressing against you, yet I would not speak to you.
Moreover, if you approach me while my body is still unadorned, I shall quickly crush you with my two arms— arms that are now stripped of ornaments and smeared with fresh unguents.
Thus addressed and pressed by her, whose voice was discordant with her appearance, he said:
"I will do so; release me, O fierce one, until my teacher has gone far away. (Saundarananda 4.37)
Then, released from her arms— which were smeared with sandalwood paste from her breasts— but not from her heart,
he cast off his attire suited to passion and assumed a form worthy of honor.
As her lover departed, she brooded over him, her eyes fixed and motionless in deep thought;
with ears pricked up and the grass cast aside, she stood like a doe whose gaze has wandered after a wandering deer.
With his mind drawn away by the desire to see the sage, Nanda hastened toward his departure;
yet, casting back his gaze, he proceeded slowly, looking at her like an elephant looking at a playful female elephant.

Gazing with a sidelong glance at that beautiful woman, whose waist was slender and whose breasts and thighs were full— resembling a golden cave of a mountain— Nanda was not satiated, like one drinking water with only a single hand.
That reverence directed toward the Buddha drew him forward, while his love for his wife drew him back;
due to this indecision, he neither went nor stayed, like a royal swan tossed upon the waves.
Having lost sight of her, he quickly descended from that palace;
yet, upon hearing the sound of her anklets, his heart was seized again and he hung back.
Held back by his passion for sensual desire and drawn forward by his love for the Dharma,
he proceeded with difficulty, being turned back like a boat going against the current of a river.
Then he set out with very long strides, thinking, "How might my pace not be too slow?
and, "How might I embrace that beloved who is so fond of her forehead-mark while its paste is still wet?"

Then, on the road, he saw the Daśabala, who had cast off pride even in his father’s city and was likewise free from arrogance, lingering all around like Indra’s banner being honored by those following in his train.
The fourth canto, titled “The Request for a Wife,” in the epic poem *Saundarananda* is completed.
The fifth canto: Nanda’s Initiation.
Then, having dismounted from their horses, chariots, and elephants, the Śākyas— each assuming a dress according to his own means—
and the merchants from the great marketplaces, out of devotion toward the Great Sage, paid him homage.
Some, having bowed, followed for a moment; some, having bowed, departed according to their business;
others remained in their own dwellings with palms joined, their eyes fixed intently upon him.
Then, on that royal road, the Buddha proceeded with difficulty through the great stream of people full of devotion,
like a river's current during the onset of the rains.
Then Nanda was unable to perform a prostration to the Tathāgata, who was being honored by great beings gathering together; yet he took delight in the majesty of his teacher.
Desiring to cast off his own attachment on the road, protecting the devotion of the people toward another leader,
and wishing to win over Nanda who was intent on returning home, the Sugata then took a different path.
Then, being himself solitary and possessing a solitary mind, he who knew the true path set out upon the path;
and having gone before him, Nanda bowed down to that most excellent one who was liberated through joy.

Advancing slowly with reverence, his shoulders draped by his upper garment, his body bent forward, with palms joined below and eyes cast upward, he spoke these words in a faltering voice: (Saundarananda 5.7)
Standing upon the palace roof, I heard that the Blessed One had entered within to bestow his grace;
therefore, filled with haste and feeling a sense of indignation toward the vast courtyards of my own house, I have come here.
Therefore, O beloved of the virtuous, for my sake, it is well that you, O best of monks, consider this the time for alms;
for the sun, desiring to reach the meridian of the sky, seems to remind one of the hour.
Thus addressed by him who was prostrate before him, his eyes upturned with affectionate pride,
the Sugata performed such a sign that he understood there would be no need for food.
Then, having prostrated before the sage, he set his mind on departing for home;
but the Sugata, whose eyes were like lotus petals, gave him his alms-bowl as a favor.
Then, for the sake of the fruit that comes from giving in this world, he, being self-restrained, took with his lotus-like hands— capable of grasping a bow— the bowl of that peerless worthy recipient.
Perceiving from afar that the Sugata’s mind was turned away and his attention fixed elsewhere, Nanda—
though holding the bowl in his hand and desiring to go home— turned back from the path, keeping his eyes upon the Sage.
When he, out of affection for his wife, was eager to depart even while holding his bowl,
the sage then bewildered him by obstructing the entrance to the street.
For the Sage perceived that Nanda possessed the seed of liberation, yet his knowledge was weak while the dust of the afflictions was intense;
since he was inclined toward the afflictions and characterized by sensual objects, the Sage drew him forth.
The side of affliction is seen to be twofold, and likewise the side of purification is of two kinds:
that which has the self as its basis belongs to one who emphasizes the power of the cause, while that which has the external as its basis belongs to one who values conditions.
But he whose causal power is superior is liberated without effort as soon as he is struck;
whereas one whose intellect is led by conditions attains liberation through effort and by means of another's support.
Nanda, whose mind was led by faith, attained a state of identification with whomever he relied upon;
therefore, the Sage, wishing to lift him out from the mire of affection, provided him with such food there.
But Nanda, struggling with grief, followed his teacher slowly and reluctantly,
reflecting on the face of his wife, with its eyes restless in their gaze and its moist tilaka-mark.
Then the Sage led him— who was adorned with lovely garlands and necklaces, who had been brought there by the month of spring,
and whose pleasure-groves for women were broken— to a monastery esteemed for its study of the sciences.
Then the Greatly Compassionate One, seeing him so distressed, felt compassion for a moment;
he touched the crown of his head with his hand, which was marked with the wheel on its palm, and spoke this to him: *Saundarananda 5.21*
O gentle one, apply your mind to tranquility before the destructive time arrives;
for death strikes down with a total assault anyone existing here in any state whatsoever. (Saundarananda 5.22)
Restrain the fickle mind from the insubstantial pleasures of desire, which are common to all and resemble a dream;
for there is no satisfaction for the world through desires, just as there is none for fire fanned by the wind through oblations.
The wealth of faith is the most excellent among all forms of wealth; the savor of wisdom is the best among all flavors;
the bliss of the inner self is the foremost among all pleasures; and the delight in ignorance is the most grievous among all sorrows.
He is the most excellent speaker of what is beneficial among friends; he endures hardship for the sake of Dharma among those with merit;
his action is supreme for the sake of knowledge among all deeds—why then should he submit to the servitude of the senses? (Saundarananda 5.25)
Therefore, choose that which is certain, free from fear, grief, and pain, independent of others, and unassailable by any;
choose that which is eternal, auspicious, and the bliss of peace. Why endure misfortune for the sake of the objects of the senses?
There is no impurity for living beings equal to old age; there is no misfortune in the world equal to disease;
there is no fear on earth equal to death. Indeed, these three must be experienced against one's will. (Saundarananda 5.27)
There is no snare equal to affection; there is no current as sweeping as craving;
likewise, there is no fire equal to the fire of passion. If these three do not exist, then you possess happiness.
The separation from loved ones is inevitable, and from that, sorrow is certain to follow;
even other royal sages, having fallen into madness through grief, wandered about helplessly. (Saundarananda 5.29)
Therefore, don the armor made of wisdom; for the arrows of sorrow cannot strike one who is conquered by patience.
Kindle your own inner fire like a small flame, so as to burn away the great thicket of existence.
Just as one who possesses knowledge and holds medicines in his hand is not bitten by any serpent,
so too one who is free from worldly attachment and has conquered the delusion of the world is not bitten by the serpent of grief.
Having established himself in yoga and fully realized the truth, he does not experience terror at the time of death,
like a hero standing in battle, clad in armor, with a fine bow and arrows ready, desiring victory.
Thus addressed by the Tathāgata, who has compassion for all beings,
Nanda, faltering within his heart yet bold in speech, said "So be it" to the Sugata.

Then, wishing to rescue him from his negligence and considering him a worthy vessel for the scripture, the Great Sage, with a mind full of loving-kindness, said to Ānanda: "Ordain Nanda for the sake of peace."
Then the sage of Videha said to Nanda, who was weeping within his heart, "Come.
Thereupon Nanda approached him slowly and said, "I will not go forth into the religious life."
Having heard Nanda’s intention, the sage of Videha reported it to the Buddha;
and having learned from him as well the state of Nanda’s mind, the Great Sage spoke further to Nanda.
O you who have not conquered your self, when I, your elder brother, had gone forth into the religious life, and our brothers followed us,
and when you saw us— your kinsmen— observing vows while remaining householders, did your mind feel no sense of spiritual urgency, or was it that you felt none at all?
Those royal seers are surely not unknown to you, who, laughing, took refuge in the forests;
having spat out their desires and longing for peace, they were never thus attached to these miserable pleasures.
Having repeatedly observed the faults in households and having heard of the bliss that comes from abandoning them,
your mind has no desire at all to leave your home, just as the mind of one about to die does not wish to leave a land beset by calamities.

O Śiva, how can you have no desire to ascend that very path when you are being led along it, like a merchant who has strayed from his caravan? For you are one whose destination is the wilderness of saṃsāra. (Saundarananda 5.40)
He who would lie down out of delusion while his entire house is burning and does not flee from it—
such a person would be heedless when the world is ablaze with the fire of time, whose flames are disease and old age.
Just as a condemned man, led forth to his execution, might laugh and chatter in his intoxication,
so too one who is being led toward death while Death stands before him with noose in hand is pitiable, being heedless and perverted in mind.

Since kings and householders alike have departed, will depart, and are even now departing, leaving behind their kin and possessions—how can there be any attachment to these transient dear ones? (Saundarananda 5.43)
I do not see anything in which pleasure exists such that suffering would not arise through its transformation into something else.
Therefore, attachment to anything is not appropriate; if it were appropriate, there would be no sorrow when it passes away.
Therefore, gentle friend, having understood this world to be fickle, like an illusion, a painting, or a magician’s trick,
abandon the snare of delusion called "beloved," if your mind intends to cut through the web of suffering.
Better is food that is unpleasant yet results in future welfare than that which is delicious but followed by harm;
for this reason, I urge you toward the auspicious and pure path, even though it is disagreeable.
Just as a nurse restrains a child and extracts a clod of earth that has entered his mouth,
so have I spoken these harsh words for your benefit, desiring to pull out the thorn of passion.
Just as a physician restrains a patient and administers even an unpleasant medicine,
so too have I spoken this which is contrary to your wishes, yet it is for your benefit and intended as a favor for the future.
Therefore, as long as this convergence of moments lasts and death has not yet arrived,
and as long as your age is capable of practicing yoga, apply your intellect to that which is most excellent.
Thus addressed by the compassionate Vināyaka, who desired his welfare, Nanda said:
"O Blessed One, I shall do all that you say; I will act exactly as you command. (Saundarananda 5.50)
Then the sage of Videha, having taken hold of him as he struggled and embraced him,
removed from his head— which resembled a royal parasol— the beauty of his hair, while his eyes were overflowing with tears.
Then his downcast face, wet with tears as his hair was being shorn,
appeared like a lotus in a pond whose stalks are bent and which has been drenched by the rainwater.
Then Nanda, his garments discolored by the decoction of tree-bark, overcome by anxiety like a newly captured lordly elephant,
appeared as if drenched by the morning sun at the end of the night— a full moon that has entered the dark fortnight.
The fifth canto, titled "Nanda’s Initiation," in the *Saundarananda* poem is completed.
The sixth canto: "The Lamentation for the Wife."
Then, when her husband had been taken away by Gaurī, and when Aratī (Discontent) had been removed from her who was filled with joy,
that very Sundarī, remaining right there upon the palace roof, shone forth at that time.
Expecting her husband’s arrival, she leaned out from the palace roof toward the window, her breasts pressing against the lattice;
facing the doorway, she hung there with her face tilted sideways, her earrings dangling.
With her necklace hanging low and her girdle swaying,
she shone from that celestial chariot like the most excellent of apsarases, fallen from her vimāna at the exhaustion of her merit, gazing longingly at her beloved.
With her forehead perspiring from exhaustion, her cosmetic paste dried up by her sighs,
and her eyes restless with anxiety, she stood there, suspecting her husband of being elsewhere.
Then, from the exhaustion of remaining seated for so long, she fell right there upon the couch;
she lay down sideways, her pearl necklace scattered, with one foot still lingering in a single sandal.
Then, a certain woman there, unwilling to see her so sorrowful and tearful,
suddenly began weeping and made a loud noise with her feet upon the steps of the palace stairs.
Upon hearing the sound of footsteps on the stairs, she immediately sprang up again;
and as if immersed in joy, she rejoiced, suspecting the arrival of her beloved.
Terrifying the pigeons dwelling in the eaves with the sound of her anklets,
she hurried up the side of the staircase in her joy, unconcerned that the hem of her fine silk garment had slipped down.
Having seen that woman and being deceived, she sighed again and returned to her bed;
with her face pale, she did not shine, like the sky at the onset of winter when the moon has lost its luster.

Distressed by the sight of her husband's absence, burning with both desire and anger, she sat down with her face resting in her hands and crossed the river of anxiety whose waters were grief. (Saundarananda 6.10)
Her face, a rival to the lotus, rested upon her hand which was copper-red like a young sprout;
it shone above the reflected lotus in the water as if it were a lotus bent down over its own reflection.
Reflecting thus according to her feminine nature, even though her husband was present before her, full of affection and facing her, she—
failing to find the truth in him who was devoted to the Dharma— imagined various things and lamented in various ways.
"Thinking, 'I shall return to you when your face-marks are no longer faded,' he made that promise to me.
For what reason, then, does my beloved, who was so devoted to his vow, now prove false to his promise?"

How can this unprecedented transformation have come upon the noble, virtuous, and compassionate one—who is ever-fearing of me and exceedingly generous—due to his own lack of affection or some transgression on my part? (Saundarananda 6.14)
Surely the heart of my beloved, who delights in pleasure and follows my will, must have become detached;
for if he still possessed passion, he would not have failed to come as a protector of my mind.
"Surely another woman, superior to me in beauty and disposition, was seen by my beloved;
for it was after making his false promises to me that he came away, abandoning me while I remained devoted. (Saundarananda 6.16)
"His devotion toward the Buddha was such that his speaking thus was merely a pretext for him to go to me;
for if he had truly felt faith in the Sage, he would have feared falsehood as he would a terrible death. (Saundarananda 6.17)

If he, having taken up the mirror while I was adorning myself with my mind elsewhere, now holds it for the sake of serving another person—salutations to that man of fickle affection! *Saundarananda* 6.18.
Those who do not wish to encounter such grief as this ought not to place their trust in men;
for where was his former devotion toward me, and where now is this abandonment, like that of an ordinary person, in an instant?

Thus, being separated from her beloved and suspecting him of something else, she spoke; and having ascended that celestial chariot in agitation, that woman, with tears in her eyes, addressed these words to her. (Saundarananda 6.20)
Even though he is young, handsome, and endowed with good fortune, prosperity, and noble birth—
if he has never before acted as your lover, you are being overly anxious when thinking that he will treat you otherwise.
Do not find fault with your husband, for he is dear to you, worthy of love, and a doer of what is pleasing.
He does not acknowledge any woman other than you, just as the cakravāka bird knows no mate but his own female partner.
Desiring to dwell at home for your sake and wishing to live for the purpose of pleasing you,
he was indeed ordained by his noble brother, the Tathāgata, with his face wet with tears.
Then, having heard that news regarding her husband, she suddenly sprang up with trembling limbs;
clasping her arms, she cried out loudly like a female elephant struck in the heart by a poisoned arrow.
With eyes bloodshot from weeping and anger, her slender body trembling with anguish,
she fell down like a mango branch broken by the weight of its fruit, her string of pearls shattered and disarrayed.
Wearing a garment of ruby-red hue, with a lotus-like face and eyes as broad as lotus petals, she—
once like the goddess Lakṣmī herself— now withered away like a lotus garland scorched by the sun, fallen from her lotus-throne.
Reflecting again and again upon her husband’s virtues, she sighed deeply and grew faint;
she shook her forearm, which was adorned with the beauty of ornaments, and her copper-colored fingertips.
"Ornaments are of no use to me now," she said, and she cast her jewelry in all directions;
falling there without her ornaments, she shone like a creeper whose clusters of blossoms have been scattered.
Thinking, "This was held by my beloved," she embraced the gold-handled mirror;
and as if angry, she vigorously wiped her cheeks, upon which tamāla leaves had been carefully applied.
Like a female ruddy goose whose mate has been wounded by the tip of a hawk’s wing, she cried out piteously,
as if vying with the pigeons perched upon the palaces who cooed with throats agitated by their warbling.
Though she lay upon a costly bed with golden limbs and feet, covered with various soft rugs and adorned with lapis lazuli and diamonds, she found no peace as she tossed about.
Beholding her husband’s ornaments, garments, lute, and other playthings,
she entered into darkness, wailed aloud, and sank down like one who has fallen into a mire.
With her belly heaving from her sighs, Sundarī was like a cave in a mountain split open by the fire of a thunderbolt;
burning within her heart with the fire of grief, she then became as if her mind were utterly distraught.
He wept, grew faint, cried out, languished, wandered, stood still, and lamented;
he brooded, displayed his wrath, scattered his garlands, tore his face, and pulled at his garment. (Saundarananda 6.34)
Hearing that Cārudantī was weeping so violently, the women were deeply distressed;
out of terror, they ascended from the inner apartments to the palace roof, like *kinnarīs* climbing to the mountain peaks.
With their faces wet and dejected by tears, like lotus ponds with moistened blossoms by the rain,
they lay down upon the ground according to their respective status and pride, burning with grief as they gazed after her.
Surrounded on the palace roof by those women, that fair-limbed lady, emaciated by anxiety,
shone like a crescent moon enveloped by lightning flashes amidst the clouds of autumn.
Among them, she who was distinguished by her speech, honored, and senior in age, embraced her from behind and, wiping away her tears, spoke these words: *Saundarananda 6.38*
For you, the wife of a royal seer, there can never be grief while your husband remains devoted to dharma;
for in the lineage of Ikṣvāku, the forest retreats are the desired inheritance.
Generally, those women were known to the bull-like Śākyas who had gone forth for liberation;
for them, whose vows of virtuous conduct were as firm as those of ascetics, their very homes were like groves of penance, even though they remained devoted to their desires.
If your husband has been carried away by another woman because of her superior beauty and virtues, then shed your tears;
for what woman of noble mind, endowed with beauty and rich in merit, would not shed tears when her heart is wounded?
Moreover, even if she were to encounter some misfortune, let there not be such tears for her;
for there is no suffering more grievous than that which befalls a woman of noble birth who regards her husband as a deity.

But now, having been sported with in comfort, healthy, established in the fruit, and seeing no calamities, you have attained the Dharma free from desire; why do you weep in distress at a time for rejoicing?
Although she was addressed in this way in many ways out of affection, she did not at all regain her composure;
then another woman spoke to her with friendly intent, words that were agreeable to her mind and appropriate for the occasion.
I speak the truth, for which I am firmly resolved: you shall soon behold your beloved.
Without you, that abode of beings will remain there, deprived of consciousness as if it were devoid of sentience.
Even while in the lap of Fortune, he would not find peace if you were not there at his side;
yet, even when dire calamities have arrived, no sorrow would come to him as long as he beholds you.
Go to your peace; restrain your tears and protect your eyes from shedding these heated drops.
That disposition of his toward you and that passion which he felt—he will find no delight in the Dharma because of separation from you.
One might think here: "Because of his noble birth and character, he will not take up the saffron robe and then abandon it.
But for one who has taken it up without self-mastery and is now facing toward the household life, what fault is there in letting go of it again? (Saundarananda 6.48)
Thus, being consoled by her young companions, that beautiful woman, her heart stolen by her lover,
fell to the earth like Rambhā facing the Draviḍa king, surrounded as she was by celestial nymphs.
The sixth canto, titled "The Lament of the Wife," in the epic poem *Saundarananda*, is completed.
The seventh canto: "The Lament of Nanda."
Then Nanda, though bearing upon his body the insignia prescribed by the Teacher’s rule but not in his heart, did not rejoice; he was filled with shame by the mental reflections arising from his wife.

While staying in the pleasure grove, he did not attain tranquility, due to the floral splendor of the month of Puṣpa, the all-encompassing assault of the flower-bannered god of love, and the state of youth that is so prone to wandering.

Standing dejected in that avenue of mango trees where bees were buzzing and clustering, he of the long arms like those of Yuga stretched himself wide; and having meditated upon his beloved, he drew [his mind] as if drawing a bow.
Receiving from the mango trees a rain of delicate blossoms like yellow powder,
he sighed deeply as he reflected upon his wife, like a newly captured elephant confined in a pen.
The remover of grief for those who seek refuge, yet the creator of sorrow for the arrogant,
he— having taken up the *aśoka* tree, became filled with grief and lamented for his beloved, whose groves were filled with lovely *aśoka* trees.
Beholding his beloved Priyaṅgu creeper— slender and dear to his beloved— seeming to flee in fear, he,
with tears in his eyes, remembered his own beloved whose face was bathed in tears and who was as fair as the blossoms of the Priyaṅgu.
Seeing a female cuckoo perched upon the peak of a tilaka tree covered in blossoms,
he imagined the white hair-tuft of his beloved as she leaned against the turret of her palace draped in white silk.
Seeing a flowering *atimuktaka* creeper that had grown by embracing the side of a mango tree, he immediately fell into this reflection: "Would that the beautiful woman might likewise embrace me."

Even the *nāga* trees, though made formidable by their clusters of flowers, did not catch his eye there— resembling trees in a wilderness to one who is suffering— as they were covered with golden buds like well-trained elephants with golden ornaments on their foreheads.

Though they emitted fragrance and possessed fragrant leaves, like Gandharva courtesans filled with perfume, they did not captivate the nose of him whose mind was elsewhere and whose nature was sorrowful; rather, they pierced his heart.

With cuckoos whose throats were crimson and peacocks with necks turned blue, and with other birds such as thrushes, all contented and overjoyed, and with bees repeatedly licking the honey, the humming of the forest dispelled his mental distress. *Saundarananda* 7.11.

There, burning within his heart with the fire of passion— whose fuel was his wife, whose smoke was discursive thought, and whose flame was darkness— he abandoned his fortitude and lamented various things.

Today I understand that those who, having abandoned their beloved with tearful faces, have practiced, will practice, and are indeed practicing asceticism—this they have done, they will do, and they are doing; it is most difficult for them. (Saundarananda 7.13)
In this world, there is no bond as firm as this: neither one made of wood, nor of fiber, nor of iron;
rather, it is this very face—so mobile and so charmingly eloquent.
For those [fetters] pass away only after being cut and broken through by one's own manly effort and the strength of friends;
yet the bond consisting of affection cannot be released except through knowledge and austerity. (Saundarananda 7.15)
I possess no knowledge that would lead to peace, nor do I lack harshness; I am compassionate by nature, yet I am full of desire.
The Buddha is my teacher, and I stand between them like one caught in the path of a moving wheel.
For even though I have assumed the marks of a monk and am instructed by my brother, the seer, who is my superior,
I find no peace in any state, like a ruddy goose separated from its mate.

Even now, that remains in my heart: how she, laughing mockingly at me as I was agitated by her glance in the mirror, spoke to me with feigned anger, "O rogue, what have you done? (Saundarananda 7.18).
The words she spoke to me with tearful eyes and a trembling face— “I am yours, whose body shall never age”— those words of that young woman still restrain my mind even today.
Having perceived his seat, this monk, dwelling by a mountain cascade, meditates composedly;
surely he is not attached anywhere like I am, for he sits thus peaceful and as if satisfied.
Disregarding the song of the male cuckoos and casting no glance at the splendor of spring,
he practices his scripture with such diligence that I suspect his mind is drawn away by his beloved.
Homage be to him, whose resolve is firm, whose curiosity and wonder have ceased;
to him who is peaceful in soul, whose pride has subsided within, who wanders about free from longing.

Who, being young in years, could possess fortitude while gazing upon the water with its lotuses and the blossoming forest frequented by cuckoos, during the month of Madhu which acts as the enemy of dharma?
With their demeanor, pride, gait, grace, smiles, anger, intoxication, and speech, women captivated the hosts of gods, kings, and sages; for why indeed would they not captivate someone like me?

For Hiraṇyaretas, overcome by desire, consorted with Svāhā; and Madhava, lacking in that very strength and creative power, consorted with Ahalyā. Being conquered by women, what then can be said of me, a mere mortal? (Saundarananda 7.25)
We have heard that Sūrya, having conceived passion for Saraṇyū, fashioned himself into a horse to please her;
and because he united with the mare who had become a horse, he brought forth those two Aśvins. (Saundarananda 7.26)

On account of a woman, a battle lasting many years took place between Vaivasvata and Agni, whose minds were obsessed by enmity and whose self-control had faltered; who else here would not be moved by the cause of a woman?
Out of desire, that most excellent sage Vasiṣṭha sent his rosary to a dog-cooker woman;
from her was born his son Kapiñjalāda, who, like Viśvāmitra, consumed the earth and its waters.
The sage Parāśara, whose arrow was his curse, consorted with Kālī, who was born from the womb of a fish;
from her, his high-souled son Dvaipāyana was begotten, the divider of the Vedas. (Saundarananda 7.29)
And Dvaipāyana, devoted to dharma, took his pleasure with a courtesan’s wife among the Kāśis—
she by whom he was struck with her foot, adorned with trembling anklets, like a cloud struck by a flash of lightning.
Likewise, Aṅgiras, the son of Brahmā, whose mind was overwhelmed by passion, resorted to the Sarasvatī river;
there his son Sārasvata was born, who became the restorer of the lost Veda.
Likewise, at the sacrifice of the royal sage Dilīpa, Kāśyapa stood waiting for a celestial nymph;
taking up the sacrificial ladle, he cast his own flowing vital energy into the fire, from which Aśita was born.
Likewise, Aṅgada, having reached the limit of asceticism yet being overcome by desire, went to Yamunā,
where he begot Sāraṅgajuṣṭa upon Rathītara, who was most wise.
Having beheld the princess Śāntā, even though he was dwelling in a tranquil forest,
the sage Ṛṣyaśṛṅga wavered from his fortitude, like a high-peaked mountain during an earthquake.
He who, indifferent to sense-objects, abandoned his kingdom to dwell in the forest for the sake of becoming a Brahman seer—
that son of Gādhi, carried off by Ghṛtācī, perceived ten years and one day as a single day.
In the same way, Sthūlaśiras, touched by the arrows of Kandarpa, fainted for Rambhā;
he who, out of lust and anger, was indifferent to all else, cursed her when she would not accept him.
And when his beloved Pramadvarā had her vital senses stolen away by a serpent, Ruru repeatedly slew snakes; yet it was not out of anger that he did so, but rather to preserve his ascetic merit.
The grandson of the Moon, marked by the qualities of fame, the son of Budha, possessing the power of a god—
having thus meditated upon the Apsaras Urvaśī, the royal sage Aiḍa fell into madness.
Infatuated with Menakā on the mountain peak due to his lustful nature,
that Tālajaṅgha was struck angrily with his foot by Viśvāvasu, like a hintāla tree hit by a thunderbolt.
When that supreme woman had perished in the waters of the Gaṅgā, King Janhu, his heart overwhelmed by passion,
blocked the Gaṅgā with his two arms like Maināka, the lord of mountains.

And King Śantanu, the lamp of his lineage and son of Pratīpa, though possessed of a glorious body, reeled from the separation from the Gaṅgā like a *sāla* tree whose roots have been washed away by the waters of the Gaṅgā; he was no longer his own master.

Grieving for that woman Urvaśī, who had been carried off by the son of Sunanda as if she were the earth itself, Somavarman— whose armor was his virtuous conduct— wandered about with his very heart pierced by the arrow of love.
When his wife died, that King Bhīmaka, of formidable power on earth, followed her in death;
he was renowned as Senāka because of his strength, a commander of armies like a god who had taken up his host.
When her husband Śantanu had gone to heaven, Janamejaya, desiring to seize Kālī, encountered his death at the hands of Bhīṣma; yet he did not abandon the passion directed toward her.
Pāṇḍu had certainly been cursed by Madana, saying, "You shall meet death in the company of a woman";
yet, though he was forbidden from serving those who should not be served due to the great seer’s curse, he did not reflect upon his own mortality and went to Mādrī.
Even such multitudes of gods, kings, and sages have fallen under the sway of women through the power of desire;
being weak in both wisdom and essential strength, how much more so am I, overwhelmed by grief at not seeing my beloved?
Therefore, I shall go back home once more and fulfill my desire according to the prescribed rites.
For the outward mark [of renunciation] is not fitting for one whose mind is elsewhere, whose senses are unsteady, and who has strayed from the path of Dharma.
Holding an alms-bowl in his hand, having shaved his head, having cast aside pride, and wearing discolored garments—
he whose mind has neither elation nor steadfastness, and no peace, exists and yet does not exist, like a flickering lamp.
He who has gone forth yet has not emerged from sensual passion, who wears the saffron robe yet is not free from impurity;
he who carries an alms-bowl yet is not a vessel for virtues—even while bearing the outward mark, he is neither a householder nor a monk.

"Even my reflection that it is not right for one who possesses the marks of spiritual lineage to abandon them once they have been embraced—that too vanishes when I consider how those other heroic kings, having left the forest of asceticism, returned to their homes. (Saundarananda 7.50)

For Śālva’s lord, along with his son, as well as Ambarīṣa, Rāma, Andha, Sāṃkṛti, and Antideva—having cast off their bark garments, they donned fine silken cloths once more; and having cut their matted locks, they wore crowns instead.
Therefore, as soon as my guru has departed from here for the sake of alms, I shall leave this saffron robe and depart from here;
for it is a burden to bear the venerable insignia when one's mind has faltered and one's intellect is afflicted.
There would be no purpose for the next world for one whose intellect is impaired, nor would there be any for this world of living beings.
The seventh canto, titled "Nanda’s Lament," in the epic poem *Saundarananda* is completed.
The eighth canto: "The Obstacle of Women."

Then, approaching Nanda—who had restless eyes, was eager to go home, and was in a state of great longing—a certain ascetic addressed him with a benevolent gaze and with loving-kindness: *Saundarananda 8.1*
What is this face, clouded with tears, that reveals the darkness dwelling within your heart?
Take courage and restrain this agitation; for neither tears nor tranquility look well together.
Feeling arises in two ways, necessarily both in the mind and in the body;
likewise, there are two kinds of physicians for these two, who are skilled in learning, medical injunctions, and practical treatment.
Therefore, if this bodily ailment is yours, let it be told fully and quickly to the physician;
for one who conceals his illness, being afflicted, soon meets with intense misfortune.
Now, tell me of this mental suffering; I shall declare the remedy for it.
For those who know the inner self and are discerning investigators are the physicians for a mind possessed by passion and delusion.
"O gentle one, if you think it may be told to me, let the truth be spoken in its entirety;
for the ways of minds are manifold, and the secrets of great lineages are many. (Saundarananda 8.6)
Thus urged by him, desiring then to declare his own resolve, he took hold of him by the hand with his own hand and entered another part of the forest. (Saundarananda 8.7)
Then, in that pure bower of creepers, fragrant with blossoms, the two sat down;
they seemed as if embraced by the tender sprouts, which were moved by gentle breezes.
Then he spoke of what he intended to do, held within by heavy sighs—
words difficult for a learned man who has gone forth to speak even to a monk whose speech is refined by sacred learning.

If this desire for my welfare were consistent with you— a practitioner of Dharma who always possesses a mind of loving-kindness toward living beings, and who, being compassionate by nature, remains steadfast even when I am unstable— then it would be truly fitting.

For this very reason, I have a particular desire to speak with you, who are a speaker of what is fitting; for I would not reveal this state of mind even to an unvirtuous person, were he to speak with a fickle nature.

Listen to this from me in brief: I find no delight in the practice of dharma without my beloved, just as a kinnara of restrained seed finds no pleasure while wandering on mountain peaks without his lover.
Averse to the happiness of dwelling in the forest, my desire is to go home; for without her, I find no peace, like a king deprived of his supreme sovereignty. (Saundarananda 8.13)
Then, having heard those words of him who was grieving while facing his beloved wife, that ascetic, shaking his head, spoke this slowly to himself: *saundarananda 8.14*
Alas, how pitiable! This fickle deer, longing for his herd, has escaped from the great fear of the hunter, yet—deceived by the sound of singing—he now seeks to enter the snare. (Saundarananda 8.15)
Indeed, a bird caught in a net was released by people seeking his welfare;
now, wandering through the forest rich in fruits and flowers, he seeks to enter his own cage of his own accord.
The young elephant, having indeed been pulled out by his mother from the uneven riverbed thick with mud,
now wishes to cross back across that crocodile-infested stream under the impulse of thirst for water.
Sleeping in a shelter infested with snakes, the youth was awakened by another who had woken up; indeed, overcome by confusion, he sought to seize the fierce serpent himself.
Indeed, a bird that has flown up from a forest tree set ablaze by a great fire still desires, out of longing for its nest, to fly back there again, free from all fear. (Saundarananda 8.19)
Helpless indeed through the swoon of passion, separated from his beloved due to fear of the hawk, the jīvajīvaka bird finds neither fortitude nor shame; he lives piteously.
Lacking self-cultivation, possessed by thirst, and devoid of both compassion and wisdom, the wretched dog indeed desires to eat again the very food it has vomited up itself. (Saundarananda 8.21)

Thus, having reflected upon him who was tormented by the grief of love and having gazed at him repeatedly, that ascetic, desiring his welfare, spoke these virtuous yet unpleasant words: (Saundarananda 8.22).
If you do not investigate the auspicious and the inauspicious, but have your mind fixed solely upon sense objects,
and if you have been born without having attained the eye of wisdom, then there can be no delight for you in the supreme good.

For one whose mind is unattached and whose self is wavering, no delight in the Dharma is ordained— whether in hearing, grasping, or retaining it, nor in the realization of the ultimate truth or the pacification of the mind.

But for one who perceives the defects in sense-objects, who is fully contented, pure, and free from pride, whose mind is disciplined in the practices of tranquility— for such a person of perfected wisdom, no delight in [worldly] things exists.
The thirsty man delights in the glory of wealth; the fool delights in the pleasure of sensual desires;
but the virtuous man, having transcended enjoyments through knowledge, delights in tranquility.
Moreover, the mind of one who is renowned, wise, well-born, and who honors the marks of his religious order,
does not incline toward the home, just as the bending of a mountain cannot be brought about by the force of the wind.
He who, having despised his own independent sovereignty over which he has control, would long for that which depends on others,
would be like one established on the auspicious path of tranquility who longs for a home full of faults.
Just as one who has escaped from captivity might, when struck by calamity, enter into bondage once again,
so too, having approached the forest, might one seek out the bondage known as the household life.

And that man who, having abandoned strife, would desire to serve strife once more—he, a fool with unsubdued senses, would abandon his wife and seek out one who is like strife itself. (Saundarananda 8.30)
Like poisonous creepers that have taken root, like caves frequented by serpents that have been disturbed,
or like drawn swords that have been grasped— women indeed end in calamity.
Women who are intoxicated bring about intoxication; women who are free from intoxication bring about fear.
Since they thus bring about both faults and fear, how indeed can they be fit for cultivation? ||| Saundarananda 8.32 |||
That kinsmen are divided by their own kin, and even friends by those who are friends—
this is because women, being base and deceitful, wander about perceiving the faults of others.
That noble-born men become wretched, that they engage in improper acts of rashness,
and that they impetuously enter the front of the army— of all this, women are the cause.
They captivate with their sweet speech, yet they strike with a sharpened mind;
honey dwells in the mouths of women, but in their hearts is the great poison Hālāhala.
Even a burning fire can be grasped; even the bodiless wind can be grasped;
even an enraged serpent can be grasped; but the mind of women cannot be grasped.
They do not consider physical form, nor fortune, nor intellect, nor lineage, nor prowess;
women strike out without distinction, like rivers teeming with swarms of crocodiles.
