A woman remembers neither sweet words nor endearments, nor does she ever feel affection; once won over, a woman is as fickle as wealth, and thus she is not to be relied upon here, just like enemies.
When they do not give, women become playful; when they give, they fall into confusion.
Toward those who bow down, they become arrogant; yet toward those who are proud, they are most satisfied.
They behave toward those with virtues as toward a master; they behave toward those devoid of virtues as toward a son;
they behave toward the wealthy with greed, and they behave toward the poor with contempt.
Just as a cow, though forcibly led away from one pasture to another, continues to graze;
so too does a woman, having gone elsewhere and disregarding her former affection, take pleasure in her new situation.
For women indeed enter even the funeral pyre, they even follow [their husbands] having abandoned their lives, and they even endure constraints;
yet they do not carry affection with their true inner being.
Those women who, in some rare instance, delight their husbands by regarding them as deities,
delight their own hearts alone by the thousands through their own fickle-mindedness.

It is said that Senajit’s daughter desired a dog-cooker (outcaste), while Kumudvatī desired the enemy of the fish (Viṣṇu), and Bṛhadrathā desired the king of beasts (a lion); thus, there is no limit to the conduct of women.

The descendants of Kuru, Haihaya, and Vṛṣṇi, as well as Śambara with his many illusory armors and the sage Gautama of fierce austerities—all these were overcome by passion stirred up by women. (Saundarananda 8.45)
The minds of women are thus ungrateful, ignoble, and unstable;
how could a wise man allow his heart to be attached to them, whose very natures are so fickle?
If you do not perceive that their hearts are small, fickle,
and inauspicious, why do you not see the impure, leaking body of women as a wretched house?
Day after day, you adorn that which is impure with grooming, garments, and ornaments; with your vision shrouded by darkness, you perceive it as beautiful and do not understand its true nature.
Or perhaps you perceive that body as impure, yet you lack true discernment;
for you perform fragrant rites for the sake of pacifying the very source of that impurity.
If ointments, collyrium, garlands, jewels, pearls, gold, and fine silks are considered excellent, then let that which is innate to women be sought among them as the pure thing. *Saundarananda 8.50*
If that Sundarī of yours were to become covered in the mire of dirt, naked, with her nails, teeth, and body hair left in their natural state, she would certainly no longer be beautiful to you today.

What compassionate person would touch a woman who flows with impurity like a cracked vessel, were it not for the covering of skin, however thin it may be—no thicker than a fly’s wing? (Saundarananda 8.52)
If you truly perceive the bodies of women as a cage of bones wrapped in skin,
yet you are still forcibly drawn by passion, then lust is indeed merciless and devoid of self-control.
Imagining beauty in what is impure— among the nails, teeth, skin, hair, and body hair—
O unwise one, do you not see the true nature and the origin of women?
Having understood that both mind and body are especially fraught with defects, O woman,
let the fickle mind that yearns for worldly existence be restrained by the power of analytical reflection.
Being learned, wise, and of noble birth, you are a vessel for supreme tranquility;
having approached it, you ought not, by any means, to break the vow again.
For one of noble birth, high-minded, fond of fame, and desiring great respect,
death is better for a steadfast soul than life itself for one who has fallen from discipline.
For just as one who has donned armor and taken up his bow becomes censurable if he flees from the battle while standing in his chariot, so too does one become blameworthy who,
having assumed the mendicant's emblem, resorts to begging for alms.
Likewise, one whose horse-like senses have been stolen by desire becomes an object of reproach.

Just as one who, adorned with the finest ornaments, garments, and garlands, wanders for alms while bearing a bow and a shimmering, variegated crown, is an object of ridicule; so too is one who, having accepted deformity and subsisting on the food of others, remains full of craving and intent upon the pleasures of the household life.
Just as a boar, having eaten fine food and even lying upon a most excellent bed, might once again run toward its familiar filth when released,
so too one who hears what is beneficial and has tasted the virtuous bliss of tranquility [might likewise return to the world].
Thirsting for sensual pleasures, one might abandon the peaceful forest and long for home.
Just as a torch held in the hand burns when its flame is fanned by the wind,
just as a serpent, impetuous with rage, bites when stepped upon by the foot,
and just as a tiger kills even when it is a cub captured within the house;
Likewise, association with women leads to manifold misfortune.
Having understood these defects inherent in women that are fixed within the mind and body,
and considering sensual pleasure to be as unstable as river water, leading only to affliction and sorrow;
and seeing the world to be as fragile as an unbaked clay vessel, assailed by death—
Form an incomparable resolve for liberation; you ought not to feel such longing [for worldly things].
The eighth canto, titled "The Obstacle of Women," in the epic poem *Saundarananda* is completed.
The ninth canto: "A Censure of Pride."
Even though he was thus addressed by that monk, he did not attain tranquility regarding his beloved;
for, thinking only of her at that time, he did not hear his words, as if deprived of consciousness.
Just as a dying patient does not accept the beneficial words of a physician who desires his welfare,
even so he, intoxicated by his strength, beauty, and youth, did not accept that salutary speech of his.
And it is not surprising if the mind of one whose self is shrouded in darkness should be overcome by the evil of passion;
for the evil of a man indeed ceases only when his darkness has become thin and reached its end. (Saundarananda 9.3)
Then, observing him thus impelled by his strength, beauty, and youth,
and seeing that he was resolved upon departing for home, that ascetic instructed Nanda for the sake of his peace.
I understand strength, beauty, and fresh youth just as you understand them;
however, I perceive these three of yours to be unstable in a way that you do not perceive them to be.
For this body is a seat of disease, subject to old age, as unstable as a tree on a riverbank;
it is as fragile as water-foam, yet you do not realize this, whereby you imagine yourself to possess strength.

Since the body is seen to be on the verge of ruin through both the neglect and the excessive indulgence of food, drink, seats, vehicles, and activities—for what reason do you maintain pride in your strength? (Saundarananda 9.7)
When the world is afflicted by misfortunes such as cold, heat, disease, old age, hunger, and the like—
wasting away like water in the bright month under the rays of the sun— why, O one proud of your strength, do you not realize this?

When this body, consisting of skin, bone, flesh, and blood, subsists only by means of food, being incessantly afflicted and requiring constant remedial action—how can you be so deluded as to think, "I am endowed with strength"? Saundarananda 9.9.
Just as a man might desire to cross the turbulent great ocean by relying on an unbaked earthen jar,
so too does one who exerts effort for the sake of sense-objects exert his strength while carrying a lofty structure that is utterly without substance.
In my view, this body is even more utterly devoid of essence than a jar made of clay;
for a jar, when held according to rule, may endure for a long time, yet this physical frame breaks apart even when well-supported.
When the elements of water, earth, air, and fire— always opposed to one another like venomous serpents—
are situated within the body and lead to misfortune, how can you, O bringer of disease, determine that there is strength?
Serpents are brought to pacification by mantras, but the humors are not to be subdued by mantras;
serpents bite only here and there at certain times, whereas the humors always afflict everything. (Saundarananda 9.13)
For this body, though long tended with beds, seats, drinks, and food, and despite its many qualities,
does not tolerate even a single transgression, since it becomes enraged like a great venomous serpent.

When one afflicted by cold resorts to fire, or when struck by the heat of summer longs for snow; when one is overcome by hunger seeks food, or by thirst seeks water—whence comes strength, what is it, how does it exist, and to whom does it belong? (Saundarananda 9.15)
Therefore, having understood that the body is thus afflicted, you ought not to think, "I am endowed with strength.
The world is without essence, without end, and uncertain; in this impermanent world, strength is unstable.

Where is that strength of the thousand-armed Arjuna Kārtavīrya, who was so proud of his might, whose arms were severed in battle by the descendant of Bhṛgu, just as a thunderbolt hews down the great peaks of a mountain? (Saundarananda 9.17)

Where is that strength of Hari, the drawer of Kaṃsa, who split the temples of the king of horses, whom Jarā struck with a single arrow—just as old age, having arrived in due course, destroys even the most excellent form? (Saundarananda 9.18)
Where is that strength of Namuci— the son of Diti, who incited the wrath of the immortals and was as fierce as a wild buffalo—
whom Vāsava slew in battle with a mere fragment of foam while he stood like the enraged God of Death?

Where had that strength of the Kurus gone when they were struck down? Having blazed in battle with speed and vigor like fires kindled by fuel at a sacrifice, they now lay reduced to ashes, their lives extinguished.
Therefore, having understood that the strength of those who pride themselves on their power and vigor has been crushed,
and reflecting upon how the world is subject to old age and death, you ought not to maintain pride in your own strength.
If you do not consider your strength to be great, then engage in battle with the sense-faculties;
for if you are victorious here, your strength is indeed great, but if you are defeated, your strength is in vain.
For thus it is not those men who are considered heroes; they do not truly conquer their enemies along with their horses, chariots, and elephants.
Rather, those wise ones are considered the truest of heroes who conquer the six restless sense-faculties. (Saundarananda 9.23)
And as for your thought, "I am handsome," O wise one—this is not so; let this also be considered:
where is that beauty, and where is that handsome body of Gada, Śāmba, and Sāraṇa? (Saundarananda 9.24)
Just as a peacock, with its shimmering variegated eye-patterns, possesses a beautiful form by its very nature, so too,
if you are truly handsome, you possess such beauty even without the quality of bodily adornment.

O handsome one, tell me, what would his body be like if he were to wear clothes contrary to custom, or if he did not touch water at the time of purification, or if he did not apply special ointments? Saund 9.26.
Observing that your youth has reached its prime, your mind is now turned toward the household for the sake of attaining sensory objects;
restrain it, for youth, like the current of a mountain river, flows swiftly and does not return.
The season that has passed returns again; the moon, having waned, comes back once more. But the water of rivers and the youth of men, once gone, never returns. (Saundarananda 9.28)
When you see your face discolored, with its beard faded, wrinkled and distorted, teeth decayed, eyebrows drooping, and luster lost—
worn out and overcome by old age— then you will be sobered and free from pride.
Having indulged for a long time in the finest intoxicating drink during the nights at the end of the day, a man becomes intoxicated;
yet no one, though intoxicated by strength, beauty, and youth, ever becomes so intoxicated as when one has not yet encountered old age.
Just as sugarcane, when its juice has been completely squeezed out, lies cast upon the ground and withers for the sake of burning;
so too the body, crushed by the machine of old age and drained of its essence, remains only for death.
Just as a saw, driven by two men, splits a towering log into many pieces, so too does old age, joined with day and night, strike down these people who stand tall. (Saundarananda 9.32)

The thief of memory, the destroyer of the body, the ender of pleasure, the seizer of speech, hearing, and sight, the source of exhaustion, and the slayer of strength and vigor—there is no enemy equal to old age for those possessed of a body. (Saundarananda 9.33)
Having understood this—old age, the guide to death and a great terror for the world—you ought not to ascend to ignoble pride, thinking, "I am handsome, strong, or young. (Saundarananda 9.34)
For those whose minds are stained by passion, there is the notion of a body, and this grasping at "I" and "mine" which you possess in this age of Kali—abandon it!
For if peace were to come, such fear would cease; yet one who clings to "I" and "mine" is beset by dread.

When no one has mastery over this body as it is being assailed by various calamities, how can it be right to regard this abode of misfortunes, known as the "body," as "I" or "mine"? (Saundarananda 9.36)
He who would always delight in a wretched house that is perpetually impure, yet constantly renovated and seemingly strong— he,
possessing perverted vision, would delight in this body which consists of foul elements, is impure, and is unstable and shifting.
Just as a wicked king forcibly takes all taxes from his subjects and yet does not protect them,
even so the body seizes all the means of subsistence such as clothing and the like, and yet does not comply with one's needs.
Just as grasses sprout from the earth without effort, whereas rice grows only through exertion;
even so, sufferings arise without effort, while pleasures arise either through effort or not at all.
For one who drags about this afflicted and flickering body, there is no happiness whatsoever in the ultimate sense;
for what is called "happiness" is merely the pursuit of a remedy for suffering, which one perceives only when that suffering has become slight.
Just as even the slightest suffering that has arrived overcomes happiness, however excellent and desired it may be, disregarding it;
so too, when suffering has come upon oneself, no happiness whatsoever exists for anyone, regardless of its quality.
If you do not understand that such a body is unstable and full of manifold sufferings for the sake of fruit,
then let the mind be restrained by the reins of fortitude from those fleeting fruits, like a cow greedy for grain.
For sensual enjoyments do not lead to satisfaction, just as oblations do not satisfy a blazing fire;
in whatever measure one indulges in the pleasures of desire, to that same extent craving for sense objects increases.
And just as one afflicted by the calamity of leprosy finds no relief from the heat of the fire,
so too one who has not conquered his senses, wandering among the objects of the senses, attains no peace through the enjoyment of desires.

Just as one might resort to diseases out of a desire for the pleasure of medicine, yet not resort to them when they have served their purpose, so too, though the body is a vessel of manifold sufferings, one may delight in it through delusion out of a longing for sense-objects. (Saundarananda 9.45)
A person who desires what is harmful to another is indeed that person's enemy by virtue of that very act;
for sense-objects, which are the sole root of harm, must surely be abandoned like dangerous enemies. (Saundarananda 9.46)
Having been enemies intent on destruction right here, they become friends to a person in the course of time;
yet sensual desires are causes of suffering both in this world and the next, and are never auspicious for anyone.
Just as the fruit of the *kimpāka* tree, though possessing flavor, color, and fragrance, leads to death when consumed and not to nourishment,
so too do sense objects lead to misfortune and not to well-being for one whose mind is fickle.

Having understood this, which is free from evil, endowed with the dharma of liberation and other benefits, and approved by the virtuous, please accept my thought; or else, speak your own decision, uttering your words. (Saundarananda 9.49)

Thus addressed by that great ascetic with words that were both beneficial and abundant, Nanda neither attained steadfastness nor found peace; like an elephant blinded by rutting-juice and overcome by excessive intoxication, his mind was darkened by passion. (Saundarananda 9.50)
Having understood Nanda’s disposition— wavering and directed toward domestic pleasures rather than the Dharma—
the monk then spoke to the Buddha, the knower of reality, who examines the intentions, latent tendencies, and dispositions of sentient beings.
The ninth canto, titled “A Reproach Against Pride,” in the epic poem *Saundarananda* is completed.
The tenth canto: “A Vision of Heaven.”
Then, hearing that Nanda was desirous of abandoning his noble vows, longing for his wife, and wishing to enter his home—
devoid of joy and stripped of fortitude— the Sage, desiring to uplift him, called out to him.
Sucitta asked him, who had attained the path of liberation though not yet reached its goal, about his lapse of mind;
he, bowing with shame before the modest one, spoke his own conviction to that master of discernment. (Saundarananda 10.2)
Having perceived that Nanda was wandering in the darkness called "wife," the Sugata took him by the hand and leaped into the sky, like a virtuous man wishing to lift a stain out of water.
Clad in saffron robes and radiant as gold, the two shone in the clear sky like a pair of cakravāka birds scattered upon a lake with their wings interlocked and spread.
They quickly reached the Himavat, which possesses the supreme fragrance of *devadāru* trees, abounds in rivers, lakes, and cascades, contains veins of gold, and is frequented by divine sages.
On that auspicious mountain, frequented by Cāraṇas and Siddhas, where the smoke of sacrificial offerings served as a mantle,
those two stood like islands in the sky, which is otherwise inaccessible on its far shore and without support.
While the Sage remained there with his senses stilled, Nanda gazed about in wonder at the caves,
the groves, and the forest-dwellers, who were both the adornment and the very guardians of the mountain.
On that long, white peak, a peacock with its plumage folded lay asleep;
it shone like a beryl armlet upon the long, thick arm of Bala.
Resting upon the rock of his mind’s virtue, the lion shone with shoulders made yellowish-gold,
like the shattered silver armlet of Ambika, variegated with patterns of refined gold.
Moving with a playful gait, though extended by fatigue, and keeping his tail curved to the left,
the tiger shone like one who had descended from heaven to offer water to his ancestors, thirsting for the mountain stream.

On a tree with swaying kadamba blossoms on the slope of the Himalayas, a yak became entangled; though he hung there, he was unable to sever the clinging tail, just as a man of noble conduct cannot abandon the affection born of his lineage.
And hosts of Kirātas, golden-hued, their bodies streaked with brilliant patterns like those of peacocks,
rushed forth from the caves like tigers springing out, resembling the volcanic eruptions of a mountain.
In every direction, throngs of exceedingly beautiful Kinnarīs, wandering through the caves with enchanting hips, breasts, and bellies, shone like flowering creepers with blossoms for their hair.
The monkeys roamed from mountain to mountain, searching for *devadāru* trees;
yet they found no fruit among them, just as one receives nothing from lords whose favors are in vain.
Then, seeing that female monkey being driven away from the herd, her face stained with crushed lac and one eye destroyed, the sage spoke this to Nanda: *Saundarananda 10.15*

"Nanda, as you look at her, which do you consider more beautiful—her form and gestures, or this doe whose sight is impaired by a single eye, or that person toward whom your affection has gone? (Saundarananda 10.16)
Thus addressed by the Sugata, Nanda smiled slightly and said this:
"O Blessed One, where is that most excellent woman, your wife? And where is this doe who causes distress to the mountain? (Saundarananda 10.17)
Then the Sage, having heard his words and perceiving some underlying motive,
took Nanda by the hand and proceeded just as before to the pleasure grove of King Vajradhara.
In that place, some trees assume their form in each season, while others, moment by moment, bear the entire manifold splendor of all six seasons. (Saundarananda 10.19)
Some were cultivating fragrant and noble flowers, as well as various intricately woven garlands and wreaths,
and ear-ornaments that seemed like rivals to their earrings.
Where the trees, with their red blossoming lotuses, shine like lamps upon poles;
and other trees, growing with full-blown blue lotuses, appear as if they have opened their eyes.
Furthermore, there trees bear garments that are of various colors, white, and illuminated by golden patterns; they are seamless, solid, and fine. Saund 10.22.
Where trees bear such ornaments as necklaces, supreme jewels, earrings, excellent armlets, and anklets—ornaments worthy of heaven. (Saundarananda 10.23)
Lotus ponds with unshaking bottoms grow lotuses with stalks of beryl, golden in color, with diamond sprouts for filaments; they are pleasant to the touch and possess the most excellent fragrance.

There, trees variegated with jewels and gold bear as their fruit various musical instruments— both long and broad, hollow and solid— which serve as playthings for the inhabitants of the celestial abodes.

There, that Pārijāta tree reigns like a king, shining with the majesty of its noble qualities as it oversteps the Mandāra trees, the Kuśeśaya lotuses, and the Kokanada trees bent down by their blossoms.
In that place, such trees that provide the enjoyments of the gods grow perpetually, produced upon the surface of the field of heaven by the tireless plows of austerity and virtuous conduct.
There, the birds had faces the color of red arsenic and eyes resembling crystal;
they possessed wings that were pale with crimson-tipped edges, and feet that were madder-red and half-white.
Furthermore, other birds known as *śiñjirikas* roam about, adorned with variegated golden plumage and clear, sapphire-blue eyes, their songs captivating both the mind and the ear.
Where birds roam, adorned by creepers that are red at their tips, golden-yellow in their middles,
and the color of lapis lazuli at their bases.
Other winged creatures named Rociṣṇavas, possessing the color of blazing fire with mouths as if aflame,
wander about casting glances with their bodies while captivating the Apsarases with their auspicious sounds.

Where those who have performed meritorious deeds—whether inferior, superior, or middling by their own actions—dwell, free from distress, undecaying, and devoid of sorrow; where they move at will, are perpetually joyful, and, being self-luminous, take delight.

There, the Apsarases, sporting about, captivate the weary minds of those rich in asceticism who had previously resolved to purchase heaven by bartering their very essence through the price of penance.

Having observed that world in perpetual festival, free from weariness, sleep, passion, grief, and disease, Nanda considered the world of men—subject to old age and death and ever-afflicted—to be like a cemetery. (Saundarananda 10.34)
And Nanda beheld that grove belonging to Indra, his eyes blossoming with wonder on every side;
and the Apsarases, filled with joy, surrounded him while looking at one another with pride.
Always youthful, their sole concern being love, they are common courtesans for those who have performed meritorious deeds;
divine and free from the faults of worldly possession, they are the resort of the gods as the fruit of their asceticism.
Some sang with deep and lofty voices, others gracefully broke lotus flowers;
likewise, others danced out of mutual joy, performing various bodily gestures as their necklaces were crushed by their breasts.
The faces of some among them shone within the forest, their earrings swaying,
like lotuses shaken by *kāraṇḍava* ducks emerging from mines where the leaves have been scattered.
Seeing them emerge from the depths of the forest like streaks of lightning from rain-clouds,
Nanda’s body trembled with passion, like the reflection of the moon in rippling water.
Then, with his mind, he captivated their divine form and graceful gestures;
and with a gaze drawn by curiosity, he felt a passion as if born from a thirst for union.

His thirst having been further aroused, longing for the apsarases and overcome by the distress of his pursuit, he was led astray by the chariot of his mind— drawn by the horse of the restless senses— and could find no steadfastness.
Just as a person makes a soiled garment even dirtier with alkaline salt—
not for the sake of removing the stain, but for the sake of producing more dirt— so did the Sage draw out passion from him.
Just as a physician, desiring to extract humors from the body, might exert himself to cause further distress,
so did the Sage, wishing to destroy his passion, induce even greater passion within him.
Just as the radiance of the thousand-rayed sun rising in the darkness eclipses the light of a lamp,
so too does the splendor of the apsarases obscure the luster of women in the world of men.
A great form destroys a small form, and a loud sound destroys a faint sound; a severe pain destroys a mild pain. Every great cause leads to the destruction of the minute. (Saundarananda 10.45)
And by the power of the Sage, Nanda was able to endure that sight which others could not bear;
for the splendor of the celestial nymphs' bodies would have scorched the mind of one who is not free from passion and is weak.
Then, perceiving that Nanda’s passion had intensified while his attachment to his wife had subsided,
the dispassionate Sage, desiring to counteract passion with passion, spoke these words.

"O inhabitant of heaven, look at these women and speak the truth as it is: how are they regarded by you in terms of their beauty and qualities, or what is that person in whom your mind has found its rest? (Saundarananda 10.48)

Then Nanda, his gaze fixed solely upon the apsarases, his heart set ablaze by the fire of passion, his mind clinging to desire, spoke these words with a faltering voice and palms joined in reverence: *Saundarananda 10.49*
O Lord, while that woman with the beautiful limbs has her gaze stolen away by him, in that very interval,
your wretched wife perceives him as a celestial nymph in bodily form.
Just as I previously had no regard for any other women upon seeing my wife,
so now I have no regard at all for her upon seeing their beauty.
Just as someone who has been scorched by a mild heat might be burned by a great fire, so too,
having first been heated by mild passion, I am now being consumed by this fire of passion.
Sprinkle me with the water of your words, lest I be consumed like the enemy of the lotus;
for today this fire of passion desires to burn me, just as a rising fire consumes dry grass along with the tops of trees. (Saundarananda 10.53)

Be gracious, O Sage; I am sinking, so release me! You possess the fortitude of the earth, yet I have no fortitude left. I shall give up my life, O one whose mind is liberated; grant the nectar of your words to me who am about to die.

For I have been bitten in the heart by the serpent of passion, which has useless enjoyment for its body, the view of frustration for its eyes, heedlessness for its fangs, and the fire of the poison of darkness; therefore, O Great Physician, provide me with the antidote. (Saundarananda 10.55)
No one bitten by this serpent of passion remained established in their own self;
for even the mind of Śaṃtanu, though wise and his body slender, became deluded, despite being of unshakable nature toward awakening.

Since you, the distinguished refuge, are present, grant this to me as I speak: act so that while dwelling here I do not wander from direction to direction, and so that having attained the end of my afflictions, I may reach the final cessation. Saundarananda 10.57.

Then Gautama, the moon among great sages who dispels the darkness of the world and has abandoned all darkness, spoke to him as he sought to strike his heart— like the moon that dispels the darkness arisen at night.
Embrace steadfastness, shake off agitation, and restrain both your learning and your mind; listen!
If you desire these women, then perform here the highest austerity for the sake of pure merit.

For these cannot be won by force, nor by service, nor by gifts, nor by physical beauty; indeed, they are won only through the practice of Dharma. If you have joy, then practice the Dharma with devotion.

Dwelling here in heaven together with the gods, amidst delightful forests and ageless women—this is the fruit of one's own auspicious karma; it was not given by another, nor did it arise without a cause. (Saundarananda 10.61)
On earth, a man may or may not sometimes obtain women through such labors as archery and the like;
but those who perform meritorious deeds here undoubtedly become [the consorts] of those of virtuous karma in heaven through the practice of dharma.
Therefore, being vigilant and striving in self-restraint, take delight if you desire the apsarases;
and I shall be your guarantor in this firm vow, so that you will certainly attain them.
From that point on, established in the thought that this was the supreme state, he exercised the highest resolve toward the Great Sage;
then the Sage, descending like the wind from the sky, took hold of him and returned once more to the surface of the earth.
The tenth canto, titled "Beholding Heaven," in the epic poem *Saundarananda* is completed.
The eleventh canto: The Inferiority of Heaven.
Then, seeing those women wandering like celestial nymphs in the Nandana grove,
Nanda bound his restless and difficult-to-tame mind to the pillar of self-restraint.
Having fixed his heart upon the celestial nymphs, he— devoid of the flavor of renunciation and resembling a withered lotus— wandered about practicing a tasteless dharma.
Likewise, having been one whose senses were restless and whose range of sensory experience was dear to him,
he became one whose senses were restrained solely through mastery over the objects of the senses.
Skilled in the ways of sensual pleasure yet faltering in the conduct of a monk,
he practiced the holy life, supported by his supreme teacher.
Through the restraint and tranquility [of his mind] and through the intensity of his passion,
he was both cooled and dried up by their union, like water and fire.
Although he was naturally handsome, he attained an extreme disfigurement through his longing for the Apsarases and by his prolonged practice of ascetic discipline.
Even during conversations concerning his wife, he who was so fond of his wife remained as if free from passion; he neither rejoiced nor was he agitated.
Knowing him to be thus established and turned away from passion for his wife, Ānanda approached Nanda and spoke these words out of affection: *Saundarananda 11.8*
"Aha! How well does this undertaking accord with his learning and his noble lineage—if he remains established in self-restraint, healthy and steadfast in his discipline! (Saundarananda 11.9)
Since this consciousness has arisen in one who is deeply attached to desires, full of passion, and whose soul is intent on sense-objects, it could not have been produced by a minor cause.
A mild disease is warded off with little effort;
a powerful one perishes—or perhaps does not—only through powerful efforts. (Saundarananda 11.11)
A mental affliction difficult to remove and powerful has arisen within you;
yet, if it has been turned back, you are in every way possessed of fortitude.
It is difficult for one who is ignoble to achieve goodness, and for one who is proud to achieve gentleness;
it is difficult for one who is greedy to practice renunciation, and for one who is lustful to maintain celibacy.
But I have one doubt regarding this firm resolve of yours; I wish for your consent in this matter, if you think it should be spoken. (Saundarananda 11.14)
A word spoken with sincerity should not be interpreted otherwise; for a virtuous person does not perceive even harsh speech as harsh when the underlying intention is pure. (Saundarananda 11.15)
For that which is beneficial is unpleasant, and that which is pleasant is not beneficial;
but that which is both pleasant and beneficial is as rare as medicine that is both delicious and wholesome.
Trust, acting for one's welfare, sharing in both joy and sorrow,
forbearance, and affection— this is the conduct of friendship among the virtuous.
This which I wish to say to you is out of affection, not from a desire to harm;
for my intention is to speak of what is for your own welfare, since I ought not to remain indifferent.
"You are said to practice the Dharma as a hireling for the Apsarases;
is this a reality, or is it some such jest? (Saundarananda 11.19)
If this is indeed true, I shall declare here whatever medicine there may be;
otherwise, I shall speak of that dust which is the arrogance of speakers.
Then, having been struck in the heart by him with gentle words, he reflected for a long time, sighed deeply, and sat with his face slightly cast down. (Saundarananda 11.21)
Then, having perceived his gesture which indicated the resolve of his mind, Ānanda spoke words that were unpleasant yet sweet in their ultimate consequence. (Saundarananda 11.22)
From your appearance, I perceive your purpose in the Dharma;
knowing which, both laughter and compassion have arisen within me toward you. (Saundarananda 11.23)
Just as someone might carry a heavy stone on their shoulder for the sake of a seat,
so too are you prepared to bear the burden of self-restraint for the sake of sensual desires.
Just as a proud ram butts another with the desire to strike,
so too is this celibacy of yours for the sake of [attaining] celibacy.
Just as merchants desire to sell their merchandise out of a longing for profit, so too is your practice of dharma like a commodity for sale; it does not lead to peace.
Just as a farmer sows seed for the sake of a specific fruit,
so too have you abandoned sense objects out of a longing for those very objects.
Just as one might desire a disease out of a wish for the pleasure of its remedy,
so do you seek suffering through thirst for sense objects.
Just as one who sees honey does not look toward the precipice,
so do you see the celestial nymphs and fail to see your downfall at the end.
With the fire of desire blazing in your heart, though you bear the vow with your body, what is this celibacy of yours, O non-celibate in mind? (Saundarananda 11.30)
Since you have existed in saṃsāra, hundreds of apsarases have been obtained and abandoned by you; why, then, do you still have longing for them?
Fire is not satisfied by fuel, nor is the salt-water ocean by water; likewise, one who possesses thirst is not satisfied by sensual desires. Therefore, sensual desires do not lead to satisfaction.

How can there be peace for one who is insatiable? And how can there be happiness for one who lacks peace? How can there be joy in the absence of happiness? And how can there be delight in the absence of joy? (Saundarananda 11.33)
If you desire to sport, therefore let your mind be fixed upon the inner self; for there is no pleasure equal to that which is found in the inner self, which is both tranquil and blameless.
There, no purpose is served by musical instruments, nor by women, nor by ornaments;
you shall delight in that state of solitude, wherever you may be, through that very joy of liberation.
Mental suffering remains powerful as long as craving persists;
cut off that craving, for suffering exists both when thirst is present and when it is absent.
Whether in prosperity or in adversity, by day or indeed by night,
peace does not arise for one who possesses craving for sensual pleasures.
The longing for sensual pleasures is painful, and there is no satisfaction even when they are attained;
separation from them inevitably brings grief, and such separation is certain even in heaven.
Even after performing difficult deeds and attaining what is hard to find in heaven,
he returns once more to the world of men, just as one returns from a journey to one's own home.
When no wholesome merit remains for one who has fallen away,
he is reborn among the animals, in the world of the ancestors, or in hell.
What pleasure does that [enjoyment] provide to one who, having consumed even the most excellent objects of sense in heaven, has fallen and is tormented by suffering? (Saundarananda 11.41)
Out of compassion for living beings, Śibi gave even his own flesh to a hawk;
yet, despite having performed such a difficult deed, he fell from heaven. (Saundarananda 11.42)
Having ascended to half of Śakra’s throne,
that former king Māndhātṛ, who had attained the state of a god in his time, eventually descended once more to the lower world.
Even after ruling the realm of the gods, Nahuṣa fell to the earth;
it is said that he attained the state of a serpent and has not been released from it even to this day.
In the same way, King Elivila, though refined by the conduct of a king,
went to heaven but fell from there again and, it is said, became a tortoise in the ocean.
Bhūridyumna, Yayāti, and those other bulls among kings,
having purchased heaven through their deeds, abandoned it again once that merit was exhausted.
The Asuras, who were formerly gods but whose splendor had been snatched away by the Suras,
went to Pātāla for refuge, grieving for that lost glory.
Moreover, even the great Indras—whether by royal sages, asuras, or gods and others alike—have fallen by the hundreds; thus, even greatness is not stable.
Having graced the assembly of Indra, Upendra, possessing the prowess of Indra,
fell to the earth from the midst of the Apsarases as his karma was exhausted, while they were crying out in lamentation.
"Alas, Caitraratha! Alas, the lake! Alas, Mandākinī!
Alas, my beloved!"—thus do the denizens of heaven fall to the earth, lamenting in their distress.
For even those who merely wish to die experience intense suffering here in this world;
how much more so for those who, having enjoyed happiness until the end, are falling from heaven?
Dust clings to the garments, the finest garlands wither, sweat breaks out from the limbs, and there is no pleasure in sitting. (Saundarananda 11.52)
These are the first signs of the falling away of the celestial dwellers from heaven,
just as ominous portents are for mortals who are about to die.
Whatever happiness arises for those who enjoy sensual pleasures in heaven,
and whatever suffering comes to those who fall from there— suffering alone is what prevails.
Therefore, having understood that heaven is undesirable, provides no protection, is untrustworthy, fails to satisfy, and is subject to decay, set your mind upon liberation. (Saundarananda 11.55)
For although the sage Udraka reached the formless peak of existence,
at the end of his karma he fell from there and will enter a womb among the animals.
Through seven years of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), Sunetra departed from here for the Brahma-world;
yet he returned once more and entered the dwelling of a womb.

And when even those dwelling in heaven, though possessing sovereign power, are subject to decay, what wise person indeed would long for a heavenly residence that is destined to perish? (Saundarananda 11.58)
Just as a bird bound by a string returns again and again even after having gone far away,
so too does the world, bound by the string of ignorance, return once more even though it has traveled far.

Just as one who has been released from bondage by a guarantor after having fulfilled the specific conditions of time might enjoy the pleasures of his home and, once the period has passed, enter bondage again;
in the same way, he reached heaven through self-restraints such as meditation, which acted like a guarantor.
When those activities are finished and the objects of enjoyment have been consumed, he draws the mind back once again.
Just as fish in a pond, their minds heedless as they dwell within the net, do not perceive the calamity born of confinement and move about in the water as if at ease;
so too do those who dwell within the world, their thoughts fixed on having achieved their purpose, meditate in heaven.
They consider Śiva to be the infallible, the eternal, their own abode from which there is no return.
Perceiving this world to be enveloped by birth, disease, death, and calamity, wandering through cyclic existence among gods, humans, hell-beings, animals, and ancestors—
[he sought] that which is a refuge, fearless, auspicious, immortal, undecaying, free from sorrow, and the deathless nectar.
For that reason, practice the holy life and abandon your wavering desire for heaven.
The eleventh canto, titled "The Inferiority of Heaven," in the epic poem *Saundarananda* is completed.
The Twelfth Canto:
Thus exhorted— "You practice Dharma with the aid of the Apsaras Vivekā"— he then spoke.
Then, because of Ānanda, Nanda fell into a state of extreme shame.
Due to his great shame, no joy arose in his heart;
because of this lack of delight, his mind turned away and could not remain fixed upon his vow.
Although he was dominated by sensual passion and was acting like one engaged in jest,
he did not tolerate those words once the cause had reached its full maturity.
And because he had previously believed heaven to be eternal due to a lack of investigation,
he now experienced intense agitation upon hearing that it was subject to decay.
His horse-like intention, his mental aspiration, turned back from heaven—
just as a great chariot is turned from a wrong path by a vigilant charioteer.
Ceased from his longing for heaven, he immediately became as if restored to health; like a sick man wishing to live who has desisted from delicious but unwholesome food.
Just as he had forgotten his beloved wife upon seeing the apsarases,
so too, agitated by the thought of impermanence, did he abandon even the apsarases.
Reflecting that even for great beings there is rebirth,
he became, through a sense of spiritual urgency, as if free from passion despite still possessing passion.
For that agitation arose for the increase of his spiritual welfare,
just as the root *edh* is recited by those who study the syllables within the list of verbal roots.
But no one could seize his mind from its steadfastness regarding sensual pleasures;
it is remembered as being like the verb "asti" (to be), which is understood to exist in all three tenses.
Moving with a graceful gait, the mighty-armed one, like a rutting lordly elephant,
approached his teacher at the proper time, desiring to express his inner state.
Having bowed his head to the Guru, his eyes clouded with tears, he joined his palms in reverence and spoke these words with some shame, his face slightly cast downward. (Saundarananda 12.12)
"O Blessed One, since you were my guarantor for the attainment of the apsarases, I have no need for the apsarases; I renounce your status as my guarantor. (Saundarananda 12.13)

For having heard of the revolving nature of heaven and the diversity of existence within saṃsāra, neither among mortals nor among gods does active worldly involvement appeal to me. (Saundarananda 12.14)
If, having attained heaven through effort, self-restraint, and discipline, they fall at the end still unsatiated, homage to that renouncer for the sake of heaven! (Saundarananda 12.15)
Therefore, having understood the entire world with all its moving and unmoving beings,
I take delight in your supreme Dharma, which brings about the destruction of all suffering.
Therefore, O best of listeners, you should explain that to me both in detail and in brief, so that by hearing it, I may attain the supreme state. (Saundarananda 12.17)
Then, having understood her disposition, as well as her faculties and their opposing tendencies, and seeing that what was beneficial had come before her, the Tathāgata spoke.
"Aha! This reflective discernment is the precursor to your supreme good; it has arisen like smoke from fire when the fire-sticks are being rubbed together. (Saundarananda 12.19)
Having wandered for a long time astray on the wrong path by means of the restless horses of the senses,
you have fortunately descended onto the right path through your unclouded vision.
Today your birth has become fruitful; today you have attained a most great gain, you whose mind, though knowing the flavor of desire, yearns for renunciation.
In this world, which delights in the storehouse-consciousness (*ālaya*), joy in cessation is difficult to find;
for fools tremble at the state beyond rebirth as if they were falling over a precipice. (Saundarananda 12.22)
People strive with the thought, "May there be no suffering; may there be happiness for me";
yet they do not realize that true happiness is the absolute cessation of suffering.
The world is attached to desires and the like—which are enemies, impermanent, and constant causes of suffering—and thus does not know the imperishable bliss. (Saundarananda 12.24)
That which removes all suffering is indeed the nectar within your own hand;
it is as if, having drunk poison, you now wish to drink an antidote at the proper time.

O you who are worthy of honor, your intended deed is worthy of praise, for it dispels the fear of an undesired saṃsāra; yet such is the fire of passion that it turns one away from the Dharma even when one is intent upon it.
With a mind unrestrained by passion, steadfastness is altogether difficult to maintain,
just as it is for a thirsty traveler who sees water that is tainted with poison.
Such an intellect as yours has become perverted by passion (rajas), just as the radiance of the sun is obscured by a fierce wind of dust. (Saundarananda 12.28)
That desire to destroy the darkness within the heart which now manifests itself is like the solar radiance swallowed by Mount Meru, only to be disgorged as the darkness of night.
And this is indeed appropriate for a mind of pure being: that you should have faith in the ultimate, subtle, and supreme good. (Saundarananda 12.30)
Therefore, you ought to increase this desire for the Dharma;
for all phenomena, O Knower of Dharma, are by necessity caused by desire.
For when the cognition of going is present, one proceeds to go;
likewise, when there is the cognition of lying down, one lies down, and when there is the cognition of standing, one stands.
When a person has faith that water exists within the earth, then, being desirous of it, they diligently dig into this ground. (Saundarananda 12.33)
If one had no need for fire, one would not have faith in it; nor would anyone rub the fire-drill if there were no need for it, yet it is rubbed when such a need exists. (Saundarananda 12.34)
If a farmer did not have faith that grain would grow in the earth, or if he were not desirous of grain, he would not sow seeds in the ground. (Saundarananda 12.35)
And for this reason, faith has been specifically called "the hand" by me; because, like a hand, it grasps the true Dharma as its inheritance.

Because it is preeminent, it is called a "faculty" (indriya); because of its stability, it is called "strength" (bala); and because it pacifies the poverty of qualities, it is described as "wealth" (dhana). (Saundarananda 12.37)
It is called "the reed" (iṣīkā) because it protects the Dharma;
and because it is so difficult to find in this world, it is described as a "jewel" (ratna). (Saundarananda 12.38)
Furthermore, when she is the cause of spiritual excellence, she is called "seed";
and again, in the sense of purifying evil, she is designated as a "river."
Since faith is the supreme cause for the arising of the Dharma,
I have therefore described it in various ways in those respective instances according to its function.
Therefore, you ought to nurture this sprout of faith;
for when it grows, Dharma increases, just as a tree does when its roots grow.
He whose vision is confused and whose resolve is weak,
his wavering faith does not lead to what ought to be done.
As long as reality has not been seen or heard, faith does not become firmly established or stable.
But when reality is seen, for one whose senses have been subdued by self-restraint, the tree of faith bears fruit and becomes a firm foundation.
The twelfth canto, titled "Discernment," in the epic poem *Saundarananda* is concluded.
Canto Thirteen:
Virtue and the Restraint of the Senses.
Then Nanda, having been won over by the great seer regarding faith,
was as if sprinkled with nectar and joined with supreme joy.
Through that faith, the Fully Awakened One regarded him as one who had accomplished his purpose;
and he, refined by the Buddha, regarded it as if the highest good had been attained.
That leader disciplined some with gentle words, some with harsh speech, and others with both of these means. (Saundarananda 13.3)
Just as gold, born from dust, is pure, stainless, and clean, and though it remains amidst the dust, it is not defiled by the defects of the dust; so too is the Tathāgata.
Just as a lotus leaf, born in the water and situated in the water, is not defiled by the water either above or below; ||| Saundarananda 13.5 |||
In the same way, the sage born in the world, practicing for the benefit of the world,
is not defiled by worldly dharmas because of his perfected nature and his stainlessness.
At the time of reproaching him for the sake of medical treatment, he employed endearment, abandonment, kindness, harshness, discourse, and even meditation; he did not act out of self-indulgence.
And for this reason, out of that great compassion, he assumed a body, being full of pity, thinking: "How might I liberate sentient beings from suffering? (Saundarananda 13.8)
Then, perceiving that Nanda was uplifted and had become a fit vessel, the best of speakers, who knew the sequence of the steps toward the highest good, spoke: *Saundarananda 13.9*
From this time forward, O gentle one, you ought to guard your conduct with faith and the faculty of energy as your forerunners, in order to attain the deathless state.
Act in such a way that your application of body and speech becomes pure—open, transparent, guarded, and without flaw. (Saundarananda 13.11)
It is "upturned" (uttāna) because it brings about realization, and "open" (vivṛta) because it is not concealed;
it is "guarded" (gupta) through its dedication to protection, and "flawless" (acchidra) because it is irreproachable.
For the purification of body and speech, and also for the sevenfold action,
you ought to refine your livelihood and conduct through purity.
By not indulging in the five faults such as hypocrisy and the like, and by abandoning the four practices that destroy one's livelihood, such as astrology and so forth. (Saundarananda 13.14)
Because he does not accept prohibited things such as life-force, vows, or wealth, and because he accepts alms that are offered, relinquished, and restricted; (Saundarananda 13.15)
Contented, pure, and gentle, with a livelihood that is clean,
one should apply remedies for suffering only so far as it leads to liberation.
For although livelihood arises from the same source as bodily and vocal action as previously observed, I have taught it separately because it is so difficult to purify. (Saundarananda 13.17)
For a householder with various views, right view is difficult to purify; and for a monk whose livelihood depends on others, right livelihood is likewise difficult to purify. (Saundarananda 13.18)
"This much is what is called morality; this is conduct in brief.
Through its destruction, there would be neither the state of a renunciant nor that of a householder. (Saundarananda 13.19)
Therefore, endowed with right conduct, practice this holy life,
perceiving danger even in the slightest faults and remaining firm in your vows.
For all actions leading to the highest good proceed by relying upon moral conduct, just as all activities such as standing and moving depend upon the earth as their foundation.

"O gentle one, let it be understood that detachment is the secret essence of liberation; the secret essence of detachment is self-awareness, and the secret essence of self-awareness is the vision of knowledge. (Saundarananda 13.22)
Let it be understood that concentration is the secret foundation of knowledge;
and physical and mental happiness is the secret foundation of concentration. (Saundarananda 13.23)
Tranquility is the supreme foundation for the happiness of body and mind;
let it be understood that joy is likewise the foundation for tranquility.
Likewise, joy is considered the secret foundation of gladness; and the absence of remorse regarding misdeeds committed or left undone is the secret foundation of joy. (Saundarananda 13.25)
The pure secret essence of the mind free from mental impressions is ethical conduct;
therefore, since ethical conduct leads to the highest state, purify your ethical conduct.

It is called "śīla" because of practicing (śīlana); practice arises from cultivation (sevana), cultivation from following instructions (nideśa), and instruction from reliance upon that [teacher]. (Saundarananda 13.27)
For morality, O gentle one, is a refuge like a guide in a wilderness;
it is a father, a kinsman, a protection, wealth, and indeed strength. (Saundarananda 13.28)
Therefore, O gentle one, you ought to cultivate ethical discipline;
for this is the foundation, and no other, for yogins at the commencement of liberation.
Therefore, establishing yourself in mindfulness, you ought to restrain the senses, which are by nature fickle, from their respective objects.
One should not fear one's enemies, nor fire, nor water, nor even lightning as much as one should fear one's own senses; for by them one is constantly destroyed.
Someone may or may not be afflicted by enemies or foes at some time;
however, everyone is oppressed by the sense-faculties everywhere and at all times.
One who is slain by enemies and the like does not go to hell;
however, one who is struck down by the fickle senses and rendered helpless is dragged there.
For one being struck by those [senses], there may or may not be mental suffering;
but for one oppressed by the sense-faculties, there is both mental and physical suffering.
For the arrows consisting of the five senses are smeared with the poison of volition;
they have thought for their nock, pleasure for their fruit, and the realm of sense objects for their flight-path through the sky.
Driven by the hunter that is desire, they strike human deer in the heart;
if they do not kill them, those deer fall, wounded by them.
Stationed in the courtyard of self-restraint, wielding the bow of fortitude and clad in the great armor of mindfulness, they must be warded off as they fall upon him.
Due to the tranquility of his senses, as if from having subdued his enemies,
he sleeps or sits happily wherever he goes, free from agitation.
For those who constantly long for sense-objects in this world,
there is no true discernment due to their wretchedness, just like that of dogs filled with hope.
The multitude of the senses finds no satisfaction through sense objects,
just as the ocean, though being filled incessantly, is never satiated by the waters.
In this world, the sense faculties must necessarily operate within their respective domains;
however, one should not grasp at the primary signs therein, nor even at the secondary characteristics.
Having perceived a form with the eye, established in the mere element [of consciousness], you should not conceptualize it as "a woman" or "a man. (Saundarananda 13.42)
If some grasping at "woman" or "man" should exist anywhere,
you ought not to pursue the hair, teeth, and so forth as being beautiful.
Nothing is to be removed from that, nor is anything at all to be added;
reality is to be seen as it truly is—just as it is, however it is, and whatever it is.
Thus, as you perceive reality as it is, which is eternally within the range of the senses,
there will be no foothold for covetousness or dejection.

Covetousness, under the guise of something pleasant, destroys the world whose nature is desire, just as an enemy with a friend’s face destroys one who is pure-hearted through sweet speech. (Saundarananda 13.46)
But resentment, which is designated as mental distress, relies upon sense objects;
through its persistence, driven by delusion and other afflictions, one is destroyed both in this world and the next.
Afflicted by both compliance and resistance, as if by cold and heat, the world whose senses are restless finds neither comfort nor the highest good. (Saundarananda 13.48)
The sense faculty does not become attached to its object, even though it has engaged with it,
as long as conceptual construction of the mind does not operate therein.
Just as fire blazes when there is fuel and wind,
so too is the fire of the afflictions born from sense objects and conceptual construction.
For one is bound by the object through unreal imagination;
seeing that very same object as it truly is, one is completely liberated.

For upon seeing a single form, one person indeed becomes impassioned, another becomes repulsed, someone else remains indifferent, and yet another feels loathing for that very same thing. (Saundarananda 13.52)
Therefore, the object is neither a cause for bondage nor for liberation;
attachment arises or does not arise according to the particularity of one's conceptual construction.
Therefore, restraint of the senses should be practiced with supreme effort;
for the unrestrained senses lead to suffering and to continued existence.

By those who enjoy the pleasures of desire, whose vision is the view of a self, whose sole summit is negligence, whose tongues are flickering with excitement, and who are serpents of the senses dwelling in the hole of the mind—poisoned by craving—no remedy is seen for them except the antidote of tranquility (*śama*). (Saundarananda 13.55)

Therefore, regarding these unwholesome enemies—the eye, nose, ear, tongue, and body—you must remain vigilant at all times through constant restraint; do not, for even a moment, allow yourself to be negligent in this matter.
In the epic poem *Saundarananda*, the thirteenth canto, titled “Virtue and the Restraint of the Senses,” is completed.
The fourteenth canto: “The Initial Departure.”
Then, having closed the door of the senses with the bolt of mindfulness,
be moderate in eating for the sake of meditation and for health.
It restrains the out-breath and in-breath, brings on exhaustion and sleep,
and indeed, food consumed in excess destroys one's vigor.
Just as food taken in excess leads to misfortune, so too food consumed in too small a measure does not lead to strength. (Saundarananda 14.3)
Food that has been eaten in too small a quantity diminishes one's accumulation, luster, energy, application, and strength as well. (Saundarananda 14.4)
Just as a scale bends down with a heavy weight and rises with a light one,
so too this body remains balanced when provided with appropriate food.
Therefore, observing one's own capacity, one should consume food that is neither excessive nor too little, even when guided by the rules of measurement.
For the bodily fire, when overwhelmed by heavy food, is extinguished like a small fire suddenly covered with a great mass of fuel. (Saundarananda 14.7)
Even a complete cessation of food is not recommended;
for by abstaining from food, one attains extinction like a fire without fuel.
Since there is no subsistence for any living beings without food, therefore food itself is not blameworthy; rather, it is conceptual discrimination that is to be restrained in this regard.
For living beings do not become attached elsewhere to a single object in such a way as they do when food is unknown; the reason for this must be understood therein.
Just as one with a wound applies an ointment for the sake of healing the wound, so too should food be consumed by one seeking liberation for the sake of warding off hunger. (Saundarananda 14.11)
Just as the axle of a chariot is lubricated for the purpose of bearing a burden, so does the wise man partake of food for the sake of sustaining life. (Saundarananda 14.12)
And just as two travelers, for the sake of crossing a wilderness,
might eat the flesh of their own son, so did that couple, though deeply distressed, consume it.
In this way, food should be consumed with discernment:
not for the sake of adornment, nor for the sake of the body's appearance, nor for intoxication, nor for pride.
For food is prescribed for the sake of maintaining the body, like a prop for a weak house that is about to collapse. (Saundarananda 14.15)
Just as someone might diligently construct and even maintain a raft,
not out of attachment to it, but rather with the desire to cross over a great flood.
In that way, the discerning ones sustain the body with its requisites,
not out of attachment to it, but rather with the desire to cross over the flood of suffering.
Just as one who is grieving and oppressed gives to an enemy neither out of devotion nor out of thirst, but solely for the sake of protecting his life; so too [is this giving]. (Saundarananda 14.18)
In this way, the practitioner of yoga provides food to the body solely for the purpose of warding off hunger, neither out of passion nor for the sake of indulgence.
And by means of mental concentration, the self-possessed one,
having dispelled sleep through yoga, should pass even the night in transformation.
If sleep should arise in your heart while you are conscious,
then do not form in your mind the notion that it is a state characterized by virtue.
O Mind, you must always maintain firmness and resolve, as well as steadfastness and valor, whenever you are being assailed by sleep.
Those dharmas which you have heard clearly must be committed to memory;
they should be taught to others and reflected upon by yourself as well. (Saundarananda 14.23)
One who desires to remain awake should always moisten the face with water, look toward all directions, and direct the gaze toward the stars. (Saundarananda 14.24)
With your senses withdrawn,
steady, and remaining under control, and with a mind undistracted, you may either walk about or sit at night.
In fear, in joy, and in sorrow, one is not overcome by sleep;
therefore, when sleepiness assails you, these three should be practiced.
You should experience fear from the arrival of death, joy from the embrace of Dharma, and sorrow from the boundless suffering of birth. (Saundarananda 14.27)
O gentle one, such a sequence of actions should be undertaken for the sake of staying awake; for life is rendered fruitless by sleep—what wise man would choose to do so? (Saundarananda 14.28)
Having transcended the serpents of the defilements as if they were snakes within one's own home,
it is not fitting for a wise man who desires to cross over the great danger to sleep.
For while the world of living beings is ablaze with the fires of death, disease, and old age, who could lie down without anxiety, as if in a burning house? (Saundarananda 14.30)
Therefore, knowing it to be darkness, you ought not to embrace sleep while the faults remain unappeased, like enemies bearing weapons.
Having passed the first watch of the three-watch night through spiritual practice, one who is self-reliant should resort to a bed for the sake of resting the body. (Saundarananda 14.32)
But lying on your right side with the perception of light,
you should sleep with a tranquil mind, having established awakening within your heart.
And having risen in the third watch, whether walking or sitting,
you should once again apply yourself to yoga for the purification of the mind, with your senses restrained.
Furthermore, regarding sitting, standing, looking, speaking, and so forth, you should maintain mindfulness by being clearly aware of all these actions. (Saundarananda 14.35)
Just as enemies cannot overcome a guarded city, so faults do not overpower him whose mindfulness is stationed at the gateway like a gatekeeper. (Saundarananda 14.36)
Affliction does not arise for one whose mindfulness is directed toward the body;
it protects the mind in all circumstances, as a nurse protects an infant.
But he who is destitute of the armor of mindfulness is a target for faults, like a warrior standing in battle without his armor against his enemies. (Saundarananda 14.38)
That mind should be known as unprotected which mindfulness does not guard;
it is like a leader devoid of vision wandering upon uneven ground. (Saundarananda 14.39)
Attached to what is harmful and turned away from their own true interests, they are not agitated even when faced with danger; in this case, the loss of mindfulness is the cause.
Mindfulness follows those virtues— beginning with ethical conduct— that reside within their own respective stages, just as a cowherd follows his scattered cows.
The nectar of immortality is lost for him whose mindfulness has wandered away;
the nectar of immortality is held in his very hand by him whose mindfulness is established within the body.
Whence can there be noble method for one in whom mindfulness is not found?
And for one who possesses neither nobility nor method, the true path is lost.
For one whose true path is lost, the immortal state is lost;
for one whose immortal state is lost, he is not released from suffering. (Saundarananda 14.44)
Therefore, when you are engaged in walking or standing, or established in such states as "I am," you ought to apply mindfulness to these and similar activities. (Saundarananda 14.45)
O gentle one, resort to a secluded lodging that is free from noise and conducive to yoga;
for having first achieved physical seclusion, it is easy to attain mental seclusion.
He who has not attained tranquility of mind and is still possessed by passion does not resort to a solitary way of life;
for, like one walking upon a path strewn with many thorns, he is harmed because he has not yet found the Path.
For an investigator who has not seen reality, while remaining amidst the manifold movement of sense objects,
it is not easy to restrain the mind, like a bull that has been dragged away from the midst of the crops.
Just as a fire, when not fanned by the wind, comes to rest,
so too does the mind, when unagitated in solitary places, attain peace with little effort.
Having eaten whatever food he finds at any time, and having put on whatever garment he has,

he dwells delighting in the Self; he who takes pleasure in some secluded place should be known as one who has accomplished his purpose, who knows the flavor of the bliss of tranquility, and whose mind is perfected.
He avoids association with others as if they were a thorn. (Saundarananda 14.50)
If, in this world that delights in duality and whose hearts are distracted by sense objects, a wise person of peaceful heart dwells in solitude free from duality,
then, having drunk the essence of wisdom like nectar, his heart will be satisfied.
Detached himself, he grieved for the world that was attached and miserable in its pursuit of sense-objects.
If, dwelling in an empty house, he always delights in solitude;
if he does not take pleasure in the arising of afflictions as if they were enemies;
and if, wandering while delighting in the self, he drinks the water of joy—
Then he enjoys a supreme happiness, even greater than the sovereignty of the Lord of the Thirty-three.
The fourteenth canto, titled "The Initial Departure," in the epic poem *Saundarananda*, is completed.
The Fifteenth Chapter: On the Abandonment of Discursive Thought.
Having assumed the supreme cross-legged posture in some secluded place, indeed—
Having straightened his body, he was endowed with mindfulness directed toward the present.
One should make the flickering mind intent upon an object of focus at the tip of the nose, or on the forehead, or indeed between the eyebrows. (Saundarananda 15.2)
If the fever of the mind— discursive thought of sensual desire— should overcome you,
it must be cast off and not tolerated, like dust that has settled upon a garment.
Although you have abandoned sensual desires through discernment, destroy them with their antidote, as darkness is dispelled by light. (Saundarananda 15.4)
"The latent tendency remains within them, like fire hidden beneath ashes;
O gentle one, it is to be extinguished by you through meditative cultivation, just as fire is quenched by water. (Saundarananda 15.5)
For they proceed from that [mind], just as sprouts arise from a seed;
by its destruction, they would cease to exist, just as sprouts do not exist when the seed is destroyed.
Having seen that for those possessed by desire, acquisition and the like result in sufferings arising from desires,
therefore cut them off at their root, as one would enemies under the guise of friends.
Sensual desires are impermanent, deceptive by nature, empty, and causes of calamity; they are common to many and should be shunned like venomous snakes. (Saundarananda 15.8)
Those things which, when sought, lead to suffering; when guarded, do not lead to peace;
when lost, result in great grief; and even when obtained, do not bring satisfaction. (Saundarananda 15.9)
He who perceives satisfaction through the abundance of wealth, the fulfillment of purpose through the attainment of heaven,
and the arising of happiness from sensual desires, perishes.
You ought not to recall here those sensual pleasures which are unstable, devoid of essence, unestablished, and whose happiness is merely imagined.
If ill will or cruelty should disturb your mind, it must be pacified by its opposite, just as turbid water is cleared by a jewel. (Saundarananda 15.12)
The antidote to those two should be known as loving-kindness and compassion alone;
for there is a constant opposition between them, like that of light and darkness. (Saundarananda 15.13)
He whose misconduct has ceased yet in whom malice still persists destroys himself with his own dust, like an elephant after bathing.
For what noble person, possessed of compassion, would wish to inflict further suffering upon mortals already afflicted by disease, death, old age, and the like? (Saundarananda 15.15)
Whether another person is harmed here by one's wicked mind or not,
the mind of that evil-hearted person is nonetheless consumed by fire immediately.
Therefore, you ought to cultivate loving-kindness and compassion toward all beings;
you should not entertain thoughts of malice or violence.
Whatever indeed a person habitually dwells upon, by that very thing his mind becomes inclined through practice. (Saundarananda 15.18)
Therefore, having abandoned the unwholesome, you ought to meditate on the wholesome,
so that it may be for your benefit in this world and for the attainment of the ultimate truth.
For unwholesome thoughts, once accumulated in the heart, increase and produce harm equally for oneself and for others. (Saundarananda 15.20)
By creating obstacles to what is beneficial, they lead to one's own ruin;
and by destroying the state of being a worthy recipient, they lead to the ruin of another's devotion.
Furthermore, you should practice non-distraction regarding mental actions;
however, O gentle one, you must never entertain unwholesome thoughts.
Whatever thought regarding the enjoyment of sensual pleasures dwells in the mind,
one does not attain that quality [of liberation], and it leads only to bondage.
Leading to the injury of sentient beings and the affliction of oneself, one falls into delusion and turbidity, and proceeds toward hell. (Saundarananda 15.24)
Therefore, you ought not to destroy yourself with unwholesome thoughts,
like one digging the earth with a sharp weapon adorned with jewels.
Just as one ignorant of its nature might burn genuine aloe-wood as if it were common wood,
so too does one destroy this human state through unrighteousness.
Just as one might abandon a jewel for a clod of earth and carry it away from an island of jewels,
so too does one who abandons the Dharma leading to the highest bliss contemplate what is impure.
Just as one might go to the Himalayas and consume poison instead of medicine, so too, having attained this human state, one should practice evil and not what is auspicious. (Saundarananda 15.28)
Having understood this, you ought to cast out discursive thought by means of its antidote,
just as one drives out a wedge from within a piece of wood with a finer counter-wedge.

Furthermore, if there should arise anxiety regarding the prosperity or decline of one's kinsmen, the nature of the world of living beings must be examined in order to bring that anxiety to an end. (Saundarananda 15.30)
Among sentient beings being dragged through cyclic existence by their own karma, who is one's own kin and who is merely a person? Yet, out of delusion, people become attached to other people.
For those who were your kinsmen have indeed passed away in past time;
and those who are not yet reached in future time will become your kinsmen.
Just as birds gather here and there at evening, so too do people and their kinsfolk come together in birth after birth. (Saundarananda 15.33)
Just as travelers take refuge in various types of lodgings and then depart, leaving them behind, so too is the meeting with kinsmen. *Saundarananda* 15.34.
In this world, which is by nature divided, no one is dear to anyone;
the world is bound together by cause and effect, like a handful of sand.
For the mother bears her son with the thought, "She will support me"; the son honors his mother with the thought, "She conceived me in her womb. (Saundarananda 15.36)
When kinsmen behave in a favorable manner toward their kinsmen, they then manifest affection; but in the opposite case, enmity arises. (Saundarananda 15.37)
A kinsman may appear as a foe, and a stranger may appear as a benefactor; people sever and create affection for the sake of worldly affairs. (Saundarananda 15.38)
Just as a painter takes delight in a woman after having painted her himself,
so too does one person, having himself created affection, come together with another person.
Those kinsmen who were dear to you in the other world are now performing your karma for you, or else you are performing it for them. (Saundarananda 15.40)
Therefore, you should not entangle your mind with thoughts of kinsmen;
in this cycle of existence, there is no fixed distinction between one's own people and strangers.
If some such thought should arise in you, "That country is secure, that one is well-supplied with food, and that one is auspicious," (15.42)
O gentle one, having realized that the entire world is ablaze with those various fires of the defects, you must abandon it; it must not be clung to by any means whatsoever. (Saundarananda 15.43)
Due to the turning of the wheel of the seasons and also from hunger, thirst, and fatigue, suffering is constant everywhere; nowhere is there anything auspicious.
In some places cold, in some places heat, in some places disease, and in some places fear excessively afflict the world;
therefore, the world is without refuge.
Old age, disease, and death are the great terrors of this world; there is no place where these terrors do not arise. (Saundarananda 15.46)
Wherever this body goes, suffering follows there;
there is no destination in the world where one who has gone is not afflicted.
Even a region that is delightful, well-supplied with food, and secure should be known as a "bad country" if one is tormented by afflictions there. (Saundarananda 15.48)
For this world, which is afflicted by physical and mental sufferings,
there is no secure place anywhere where one might go and be at ease.
Since suffering exists everywhere, for everyone, and at all times,
O gentle one, do not direct desire or passion toward the variegated wonders of the world.
When your desire and passion for that have ceased,
you will then regard the entire world of the living as if it were ablaze.
Now, if some thought should arise in you that takes its refuge in immortality,
it must be destroyed with effort, just like a disease that has arisen within one's own body.
One must not place trust in life for even a moment;
for Time, like a lurking tiger, is the slayer of those who are heedless.
"It does not behove you to think, 'I am strong' or 'I am young';
for death strikes down all who are unwell, regardless of their age. (Saundarananda 15.54)
For one who perceives the true goal and drags about this body, which is a field for misfortunes,
neither hope for health nor hope for life arises.
Who could possibly exist as a body, bearing this foundation of the great elements,
which is like a vessel for things that are mutually contradictory, such as the earth?
"Understand this marvel: that this human being breathes out immediately after he breathes in; for life is indeed not to be trusted. (Saundarananda 15.57)
This is another marvel:
that one who has slept wakes up, or having risen, sleeps again; for embodied beings have many enemies.
Who could place their trust in Death, who follows the world from the very moment of conception with the intent to destroy it, like one with a raised spear against his enemies?
A person born into this world, though learned and powerful, does not conquer Death;
no one has ever conquered him, nor will anyone ever conquer him.
For impetuous death, once it has arrived, cannot be repelled by conciliation, bribery, sowing dissension, force, or restraint. (Saundarananda 15.61)
Therefore, you should not place your trust in this flickering life;
for Time constantly carries one away and does not wait for old age.
For one who perceives the world as devoid of essence, like a bubble on water,
what person with a sane mind would harbor thoughts of immortality?
Therefore, my friend, for the sake of abandoning these discursive thoughts, you ought briefly to take mindfulness of breathing as your object.
By this practice, you should apply yourself at the proper time to the antidotes to discursive thoughts, just as one applies remedies to diseases.

Just as gold-washers, for the sake of gold, first discard the large grains of sand and then, for the sake of purifying that [gold], abandon even the fine particles once they have extracted the pure fragments of gold; so too does he proceed. *Saundarananda* 15.66.

With a mind disciplined for the sake of liberation, having first abandoned gross faults, he abandons even the subtle ones for the sake of that purification; having purified the constituent parts of phenomena, he attains mastery.
Just as a smith here repeatedly heats and refines gold that is obstructed by dross with water until it is purified by degrees in the fire,
so too does the practitioner of yoga here skillfully [refine] that which is obstructed by defects.
Having purified it from the afflictions, he calms the mind and draws it inward.
Just as a goldsmith brings forth various kinds of ornaments from gold— which, by its own nature, provides the basis for pleasure in craftsmanship—
so too does a monk whose mind is purified bring forth even the supernormal powers (abhijñā) under his own control.
