It calms the mind as it wishes and directs it wherever it desires.
The fifteenth canto, titled “The Abandonment of Discursive Thought,” in the epic poem *Saundarananda* is completed.
The sixteenth canto: The Noble Truths.
Thus, by means of mental concentration, gradually removing some things and establishing others,
the yogi, having attained the four meditations, necessarily acquires the five superknowledges.

The preeminent supernormal powers in their many forms, the comprehension of the mental conduct of others, the long-term recollection of past births, and the divine, purified ear and eye of wisdom. (Saundarananda 16.2)
Beyond this, he applies his mind to the investigation of reality for the sake of the destruction of the outflows;
for from that, he correctly understands the four truths, beginning with suffering, as they truly are.
This suffering is of the nature of affliction; this is the cause of suffering, being of the nature of its origin;
this is the destruction of suffering, being of the nature of liberation; and this is the path leading to peace, being of the nature of protection.
Having thus understood the noble truths with wisdom and having correctly penetrated them all four, one overcomes all taints through cultivation; having attained peace, one is not born again.
For due to the lack of understanding and lack of penetration regarding these four which constitute reality,
the world mounts the swing of saṃsāra, passing from existence to existence and never attaining peace.
Therefore, understand that birth is, in brief, the root of calamities such as old age and the very essence of suffering;
for this birth is the field of all misfortunes, just as the earth is the source of all medicinal herbs.

For that which is the birth of suffering—of this manifold form together with its sense faculties—is the very same as the arising of this physical body, and the arising of death and disease. (Saundarananda 16.8)

Just as food mixed with poison leads to destruction and not to sustenance, whether it be good or bad, so too in this world every birth—whether among animals, above, or below—leads only to suffering and not to happiness. (Saundarananda 16.9)
When activity exists, the manifold misfortunes such as old age and the like prevail over living beings;
for even when terrible winds blow, trees that have not yet sprouted do not sway.
Just as the wind has its source in space, as fire lies within the womb of the śamī tree,
and as water dwells within the earth, so too does suffering have its source in the mind and the body.

Just as fluidity is the inherent nature of water, solidity of the earth, motion of the wind, and constant heat of fire, so too is suffering the inherent nature of both the body and the mind. (Saundarananda 16.12)
When there is a body, there is the suffering of disease, old age, and so forth, as well as hunger, thirst, rain, heat, cold, and the like;
when the mind is dependent on form and accompanied by its continuations, there is the suffering of grief, discontent, anger, fear, and so forth.
Having perceived directly the suffering of birth, know that suffering likewise exists in the past;
and just as that suffering and this suffering are suffering, understand that suffering in the future is also the same.

For just as the nature of a seed is seen here, whether it has already sprouted or is yet to come, so too is it to be inferred; and just as fire is perceived to be hot, whether it has already been so or is yet to be so, it is indeed hot in both cases.
O you of noble conduct, wherever the manifestation of that name-and-form occurs in accordance with its qualities, there alone is suffering;
for that which is free from it will not become suffering, nor has it ever been suffering, nor will it ever be.
And for that suffering of worldly involvement, the collection of defects such as craving is the cause;
neither God, nor primordial nature, nor time, nor water, nor inherent existence, nor fate, nor chance is the cause. (Saundarananda 16.17)
And for this reason it should be understood that the world’s engagement [with existence] proceeds from defects;
for those possessed of passion (*rajas*) and darkness (*tamas*) die, whereas one who is free from passion and darkness is not born again. (Saundarananda 16.18)
When there is a particular desire, the application of vehicles, seats, and so forth occurs here and there;
therefore, it should be understood that the birth of living beings occurs in exactly that way through the power of craving.

"Beholding beings who are under the sway of attachment, exceedingly devoted to their own kind due to the force of habituation, know that they have been brought about by those very same defects. (Saundarananda 16.20)
Just as a distinction arises here in the physical bases through anger, joy, and so forth,
even so, in successive births, a distinction produced by the afflictions does not arise in a uniform manner.
In a birth where the afflictions (doṣa) predominate, a powerful affliction arises; in one who is passionate, intense passion arises;
and where delusion (moha) predominates, there is an excess of the power of delusion; likewise, when those afflictions are slight, the resulting affliction is slight.
For just as one directly perceives the kind of fruit that is present, one thereby understands the past seed;
and having understood the nature of the seed, one directly anticipates that future fruit.
In whichever births one’s defects have been exhausted through detachment, one is not born there again;
however, wherever a latent tendency toward defects remains, there one is reborn against one’s will. (Saundarananda 16.24)

O gentle one, having understood that craving and the like are the causes of that manifold birth, cut them off if you desire liberation from suffering; for the cessation of the effect results from the complete destruction of the cause.
Through the exhaustion of suffering and the complete destruction of its cause, realize for yourself that Dharma which is peaceful and auspicious—
the fading away of craving, the refuge, cessation, eternal, the protection, the invincible, and the noble.
That state wherein there is no birth, no old age, no death, no diseases, no union with the unpleasant,
no loss of what is desired, and no separation from what is dear— that is the secure, ultimate, and immutable state.

Just as a lamp that has reached its extinction goes neither to the earth nor to the atmosphere, nor to any cardinal or intermediate direction, but simply attains peace through the exhaustion of its oil; so too does the Tathāgata.
Thus, the one who has accomplished his task and attained final liberation goes neither to the earth nor to the atmosphere;
he goes to no cardinal direction nor to any intermediate direction, but through the destruction of the afflictions, he attains sole peace.
The means for its attainment is the path consisting of threefold wisdom and twofold tranquility;
that should be cultivated according to rule by the wise one, established in pure morality headed by the three [trainings].

Right action of speech together with right action of body, and a livelihood that is pure according to the rule—these three, engaged in the practice of conduct, are based on ethical discipline for the sake of undertaking [wholesome] karma. (Saundarananda 16.31)
Regarding the truths such as suffering and the rest, there is the noble vision, right reflection, and exertion;
these three, engaged in the method of knowledge and based upon wisdom, lead to the complete destruction of the afflictions.

Right mindfulness and right concentration, joined with logic for the realization of truth—these two, engaged in the practice of yoga, rely on tranquility for the mastery of the mind. (Saundarananda 16.33)
Virtue does not allow the sprouts of affliction to spread, just as past time does not allow the sprouts of a seed to grow;
for when a person's virtue is pure, their faults cannot overcome them, just as modesty restrains the mind.
But concentration restrains the afflictions, just as a mountain checks the forceful currents of great rivers;
for when concentration is established, the faults do not overpower him, like serpents bound by a mantra. (Saundarananda 16.35)
Wisdom, however, destroys all faults without exception, just as a mountain stream in the rainy season uproots the trees on its banks;
once burnt by it, the faults cannot arise again, just as trees cannot grow where they have been struck by a thunderbolt fire.
Having thoroughly penetrated this noble eightfold path, which is clear and unsurpassed, consisting of these three aggregates,
one abandons the faults that are the causes of suffering and attains that state of ultimate peace.
In its practice, there are steadfastness and straightforwardness, modesty and vigilance, and solitude;
as well as fewness of desires, contentment, lack of attachment, a lack of delight in worldly activities, and patience. (Saundarananda 16.38)
For he who understands suffering according to its true nature, as well as its origin and its cessation,
attains peace by means of the Noble Path while dwelling together with virtuous friends.
He who, being afflicted by disease, correctly understands the illness, its cause, and its remedy,
will indeed attain health before long when attended by knowledgeable friends.
Therefore, form the perception of a disease regarding the truth of suffering; likewise, form the perception of the cause of disease regarding its defects.
Form the perception of health regarding the truth of cessation, and the perception of medicine regarding the truth of the path.
Therefore, understand that suffering arises from active engagement, and recognize the defects that cause it to proceed;
attain cessation through withdrawal, and likewise understand the path that brings about that cessation.
Therefore, while your head and garments are ablaze, you must deliberate with wisdom for the sake of awakening to the truth;
for if one does not see the world as it truly is, it has already been burned, is being burned now, and will continue to burn.
Whenever one perceives that name-and-form is subject to decay, that vision of his is correct;
and seeing correctly, he attains disenchantment, and through the destruction of delight, passion comes to an end. (Saundarananda 16.44)
I declare that through the destruction of both delight and passion, the mind is perfectly liberated;
with the mind perfectly liberated from those two, there is nothing further for it to do.

For one who understands name-and-form according to their own nature, as well as its cause and its cessation, and who truly sees this, I declare that there is the complete destruction of the outflows. (Saundarananda 16.46)
Therefore, O gentle one, having exerted supreme vigor, strive quickly for the complete destruction of the outflows,
while specifically examining the elements as suffering, impermanent, and selfless.

For he who understands the six elements—earth, water, fire, and the rest—both in their general nature and by their own specific characteristics, and understands nothing other than them, understands ultimate liberation from them. (Saundarananda 16.48)
Furthermore, one who is determined to abandon the afflictions must examine both the proper time and the appropriate means;
for even spiritual practice, if performed at the wrong time or without the right means, leads to harm rather than to its intended virtue.
If one were to milk a cow that has not yet given birth, one would obtain no milk through milking at the wrong time;
or even at the right time, one would not obtain milk if, out of delusion, one were to milk the cow from its horn.
One who desires fire from wet wood will not obtain it even with great effort;
nor does one obtain fire from dry wood by merely throwing it down, if it is done without the proper means.
Having duly examined the place and time, as well as the measure and means for yoga,
and having carefully considered one's own strength and weakness, an effort should be made that is not contrary to those factors.
That sign which was described as "grasping," when the mind is being uplifted, should not be cultivated;
for in this way the mind does not attain tranquility, like a fire fanned by a strong wind. (Saundarananda 16.53)
Whatever cause is certain for the sake of tranquility when the mind has become agitated—that is the time for it;
for in this way the mind attains peace, just as a blazing fire is extinguished by water.
That cause which brings about tranquility must be cultivated even when the mind is dissolving;
for in this way, the mind repeatedly falls into dissolution like a weak fire that is not fanned.
That which is a fixed, uplifting sign is the proper time when the mind has fallen into laxity;
for in that way the mind becomes capable of action, like a dying fire fanned by fuel. (Saundarananda 16.56)
Nor is a state of equanimity desired when the mind has fallen into lethargy or is agitated;
for if neglected in such a state, it produces intense harm, like an untreated disease in a patient. (Saundarananda 16.57)
When the mind has attained equanimity, that is the time for the sign fixed upon equanimity;
for in this way the application becomes effective for its task, like a chariot drawn by well-trained horses. (Saundarananda 16.58)
Even when the mind is agitated by the surge of passion, the practice of cultivating loving-kindness (*maitrī*) should not be performed;
for one whose nature is dominated by passion becomes deluded by loving-kindness, just as one suffering from phlegm is further confused by consuming oily food.
When the mind is agitated by passion, one should attain steadfastness and cultivate the sign of the unattractive;
for one whose nature is dominated by passion finds relief in this way, just as one whose nature is dominated by phlegm finds it by consuming something dry.
When the fault of malice has arisen in the mind, one should not cultivate an unwholesome object;
for to one whose nature is hatred, the unwholesome leads to destruction, just as a sharp medical treatment would to one whose constitution is dominated by bile.
But when the mind is agitated by the fault of malice, one should cultivate loving-kindness by bringing it under the influence of one's own side;
for loving-kindness serves to pacify a hateful nature, just as cooling treatment does for a bilious temperament.
When the movement of the mind is bound by delusion, both loving-kindness and the meditation on the foul become ineffective.
For through those two, one falls back into further confusion, just as one who is of a windy nature becomes worse when subjected to something dry.
When the activity of the mind is characterized by delusion, one should cultivate the dwelling in the principle of "this-conditionality" (idampratyayatā);
for when the mind is bewildered, this is the path to peace, just as an oily treatment is for a wind-disorder.

Just as a goldsmith here blows upon the gold placed in the mouth of a furnace at the proper time, sprinkles it with water at the proper time, and gradually leaves it alone at the proper time; so too [should one treat the mind].
For one should heat gold at the proper time while blowing upon it; at the improper time, one should quench it by casting it into water.
Nor should one, through neglect, fail to bring it to perfect maturity at the improper time.
One must correctly observe with the mind the signs for exertion, for tranquility, and likewise for equanimity at the proper time; for even effort is ruinous if it is not preceded by the right means.
Thus the Sugata spoke to him concerning both the turning away from what is improper and the proper way;
and further, having understood his various activities, he taught the means for the destruction of discursive thoughts.
Just as a physician prescribes a remedy for the pacification of whichever humor— bile, phlegm, or wind— has become provoked, so too did the Buddha prescribe a remedy for the humors.

If one does not destroy the unwholesome thoughts through a single eon because they have become so well-habituated, then one should begin a second successive eon; for a virtuous application should never be abandoned.
Because the multitude of afflictions has accumulated over beginningless time and is thus exceedingly powerful,
and because correct application is difficult to achieve, these faults cannot indeed be severed all at once.
Just as a man skilled in that art might extract a large splinter by means of another, smaller splinter,
so too should one cast away that very unwholesome mental sign by cultivating another sign.
Nevertheless, if unwholesome thought does not subside because one is still a novice in regard to the inner self,
it must be abandoned by examining its faults, just as a traveler abandons a path infested with wild beasts.
Just as one afflicted by hunger, desiring to live, does not wish to eat food mixed with something disagreeable,
even so the wise man, realizing it brings harm, abandons an inauspicious sign.
For who is able to restrain one who does not perceive a fault as a fault?
And he who perceives a virtue as a virtue in whatever it may be, proceeds toward it even when being restrained. (Saundarananda 16.75)
For those born of noble lineage feel shame when unwholesome mental activities proceed;
just as a wise, handsome youth feels ashamed when impure, unseen things cling about his neck.

If unwholesome thoughts should persist even in the slightest degree despite being shaken off, one should employ other activities such as the practice of study and so forth; this method should be cultivated for the sake of forgetting them.
Even if one must sleep, the wise person should do so, or even undergo physical exhaustion;
however, one should never intentionally contemplate an improper object, for by being attached to it, misfortune arises.
For just as one who is afraid of thieves at night would not wish to open his door even to loved ones,
so the wise man withdraws his application equally from both the virtues and the faults of the unwholesome.
If, even when being restrained by such means as these, they do not turn back,
then they should be abandoned— just as the defects of gold are removed— by means of a thorough eradication of their grosser forms.
Just as a man, weary of the harsh application of sensual pleasures beginning with rapid journeys,
resorts to [a place of rest], so too should one proceed even regarding the faults [of sense objects] by means of wisdom.
If those unwholesome thoughts do not subside because their antidotes have not been attained,
they must not be tolerated even for a moment, like serpents in one's home that remain unchecked.

Even by pressing tooth against tooth, or even by pressing the tip of the palate with the tongue, and by restraining the mind with the mind, you must exert effort; for they do not submit to you of their own accord.
What is surprising in this, that one who is free from delusion, having gone to the forest with a composed mind, should not be bewildered?
He who is not shaken when being provoked in his heart by the causes of such delusion—he is the one who has achieved his purpose; he is the steadfast man.

Therefore, first purify the path by this method for the sake of attaining the Noble Truths, just as a king who has set out on a journey desires to conquer unconquered fortune in order to subdue his enemies. *Saundarananda* 16.85.
These auspicious forests all around are conducive to yoga and undisturbed by people;
having achieved mere physical seclusion, devote yourself to the path for the abandonment of the afflictions.
Kauṇḍinya, Nanda, Kṛmila, Aniruddha, Tiṣya, Upasena, Vimala, and Rādha; Bāṣpa, Uttara, Dhautaki, Moharāja, Kātyāyana, Dravya, and Pilindavatsa.
Bhaddāli, Bhadrāyaṇa, Sarpadāsa, Subhūti, Godatta, Sujāta, Vatsa,
Saṃgrāmajit, Bhadrajit, Aśvajit, Śroṇa, Śoṇa, and Koṭikarṇa.
Kṣema, Ājita, Nandaka, Nanda, Mātṛ, Upāli, Vāgīśa, Yaśas,
Yaśodā, Mahāhvaya, Valkalin, Rāṣṭrapāla, Sudarśana, Svāgata, and Medhika.
He was Kapphiṇa, Kāśyapa, Auruvilva, Mahā-Kāśyapa, Tiṣya, and Nanda;
Pūrṇa, Pūrṇa, and that Pūrṇaka, as well as Śoṇāparānta—that very Pūrṇa.
Śāradvatīputra, Subāhu, Cunda, Kondeya, Kāpya, Bhṛgu, Kuṇṭha, Dhāna,
Śaivala, Revata, Kauṣṭhila, he of the Maudgalya clan, and Gavāmpati.
That very prowess which you displayed in the practice of yoga, perform it again quickly and according to the rule;
then you will surely attain the state reached by them, as well as glory encompassed by happiness.
Just as a substance may be pungent by its taste yet sweet when digested after being consumed,
so too his vigor was pungent through exertion, yet its result was sweet for the accomplishment of his goal.
For energy is the supreme root in the accomplishment of what is to be done; without energy, there is no success whatsoever.
From energy arises all prosperity in this world, while the absence of energy results in every kind of evil.
The failure to obtain what has not been gained, the certain loss of what has already been obtained, self-contempt, wretchedness before those who are superior, humiliation,
lack of luster, darkness, and the cessation of learning, discipline, and contentment.
For men who lack vigor, there occurs downfall and ruin.
Having heard this method, he is unable to attain further growth;
having known the supreme Dharma, he does not find a higher dwelling;
and having abandoned the home for liberation, he does not find peace.
In this matter, the cause of a person's failure is laziness; it is not an external enemy.
If one digs the earth with undiminished zeal, one finds water;
by continuously rubbing the fire-drills, one produces fire.
Indeed, those who apply themselves to yoga certainly obtain the fruit of their exertion.
For rivers, flowing swiftly and constantly, indeed break even through mountains.
Having ploughed the earth and protected the cattle through hundreds of labors, one enjoys the splendor of the harvest;
having diligently plunged into the waters of the ocean, one sports with the splendor of jewels;
and having struck down the prowess of enemies with arrows, one enjoys the sovereignty of a lord of men.
Exert that energy for the sake of peace; for when energy is disciplined, all spiritual powers arise.
The sixteenth canto, titled "The Noble Truths," in the epic poem *Saundarananda* is completed.
The seventeenth canto: "The Attainment of the Deathless."
Then Nanda, having been thus instructed in the path to reality and having attained the path to liberation,
bowed down to his teacher with his whole being and went to the forest to abandon the afflictions.
There he saw a peaceful clearing, carpeted with soft, blue-green grass and surrounded by groves of trees,
embraced by a silent river flowing with water as blue as beryl.
Having performed the purification of his feet there at the base of a pure, auspicious, and glorious tree,
he girded his loins with the resolve for liberation and sat down in the cross-legged posture, holding his body upright.
Having set his body straight and composed, having established mindfulness directed toward the body,
and having withdrawn all his senses within himself, he applied himself with diligence to that yoga.
Then, desiring to realize the entirety of reality and wishing to perform the practices conducive to liberation,
he proceeded upon the ground for the cultivation of the mind through knowledge, virtuous conduct, and tranquility.
Having summoned fortitude, applied energy, cast off attachment, and grasped his own power,
he became one whose mind was tranquil, whose mind was established in self-restraint, who was at ease, and thus indifferent toward sense-objects.
Even though his intellect was ardent and his self was resolutely applied, the notion of sensual desire— due to long-standing habituation—
threw his mind into confusion, like lightning appearing amidst the clouds when the rains have arrived.
Recognizing her as a state of obsessive possession that obstructs the Dharma, the wise man immediately cast her aside—
even though she was his beloved— just as one whose mind is overwhelmed by anger rejects a woman of noble character who has become perverse.

But for him who had exerted vigor for the sake of mental tranquility, an unwholesome thought arose once more, like a terrible affliction befalling one intent on destroying a disease. (Saundarananda 17.9)

To counteract that [obstacle], he resorted to another wholesome means conducive to yoga, like one whose strength is exhausted being driven out by a powerful enemy who stands firm. (Saundarananda 17.10)

Just as a king, having established his city, applied his authority, won over friends, and subdued his enemies, thereby acquires previously unattained land—such indeed is the policy for one who seeks liberation in yoga. (Saundarananda 17.11)
For the yogin who desires liberation, the city is the mind, the method of knowledge is the staff, virtues are his friends, and faults are his enemies; he strives for that purpose which is liberation.
Desiring to be liberated from the great web of suffering and wishing to enter upon the attainment of the path to liberation,
he went toward tranquility with his eyes somewhat opened, desiring to behold the supreme path of the Muni.
He who would be a dwelling place for darkness is homeless even after hearing the truth; he remains heedless.
But because he is a fit vessel for liberation, he withdrew his mind within his own self. (Saundarananda 17.14)

Then the self-possessed one duly conducted an investigation into phenomena according to their equipment, conditions, intrinsic nature, gratification, specific defects, and likewise their nature as an escape. (Saundarananda 17.15)
Desiring to see the essence of both the material and the immaterial, he scrutinized the body;
then he scrutinized the body as indeed impure, suffering, impermanent, non-self, and devoid of a soul.
There, by means of the supreme mundane path, he caused the tree of the afflictions to tremble through its impermanence, its emptiness, its selflessness, and its very suffering.
"Since everything here comes into being after not having been, and having come into being, it necessarily ceases to exist again;
and since it has a cause and is subject to decay because of that cause, he concluded that the world is impermanent."
Since for one who is born, engagement in action— which is the cause of bondage and the destruction [of liberation]—
is inevitably entailed in the pursuit of what is called pleasure as a means of remedying suffering, he therefore perceived worldly existence itself to be suffering.
And since that which belongs to the conditioned is solitary, with no agent or experiencer whatsoever,
and since its activity arises from a causal complex, he therefore beheld this world as empty.
Because the world is devoid of effort and lacks independence, such that no single being exercises sovereignty over actions;
and because various phenomena arise in dependence upon those very conditions—he therefore understood the world to be without self.

Then, like one fanning for wind on a hot day, or producing fire from wood by friction, or digging for water within the earth, he attained the world-transcending path that is so difficult to reach. *Saundarananda 17.22*
Having strung the bow of right knowledge and donned the armor of mindfulness, standing firm upon the mount of pure ethical discipline and vows,
he stood ready for victory, desiring to fight against the enemies of the afflictions stationed on the battlefield of the mind.
Then, having taken up the sharp weapons of the factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) and mounted upon the supreme vehicle of the right efforts (samyakpradhāna),
he gradually plunged into the army of the afflictions with a force consisting of the elephants that are the limbs of the path (mārgāṅga).

With arrows consisting of the applications of mindfulness, he instantly shattered his enemies— the four causes of suffering composed of perversion— by means of their respective four spheres of activity.
With the five incomparable noble powers, he shattered the five mental wastelands;
likewise, with the eight noble paths, he utterly drove away the eight serpents of false views.
Then, having shaken off every view of a self and being free from doubt regarding the Four Truths, he—
purified in his observance of moral precepts and vows and having realized the Dharma— attained the first stage of the fruit of the Dharma.
Because of his separation from a portion of the afflictions through the vision of the four noble truths,
and because of his personal attainment of excellence and the direct experience of the bliss of the wise, he [is liberated].
Due to the firmness of his serene confidence, the stability of his fortitude, his lack of delusion regarding the four truths,
and the flawlessness of his supreme ethical conduct, he became free from doubt concerning the method of the Dharma.
Freed from the net of false views and beholding the world as it truly is,
he attained a joy rooted in knowledge and experienced even greater clarity of faith toward his teacher.
For he who understands that the process of existence is determined, occurring neither from another cause nor without a cause,
and who realizes each thing in dependence upon its respective conditions— he beholds the ultimate, noble Dharma.
He who perceives the Dharma— peaceful, auspicious, ageless, dispassionate, and the supreme good—
then beholds its teacher, the most excellent of the noble ones, the Buddha who has attained the eye of wisdom.

Just as one freed from disease by the instruction of a skilled physician looks upon that physician with a mind of gratitude, so too does the healthy man, mindful of his deliverance from illness, behold him with a vision of the heart, satisfied both by his friendliness and his knowledge of the science.

Liberated by the noble path, the Knower of Reality, having realized the noble truth, beholds the Tathāgata through recollection; as a bodily witness, he is satisfied by his loving-kindness and his omniscience.

Freed from destructive views and having perceived the end of renewed existence, he cast off all aversion toward the manifestations of the afflictions; he feared neither death nor the miserable realms.
Filled with a collection of impurities— skin, sinews, fat, blood, bone, flesh, hair, and so forth—
he, upon closely examining that body, sought its essence but did not find even an atom of it.
With a steadfast mind, he thinned out both sensual desire and aversion by that very yoga;
having made those two thin upon his broad-chested body, he attained the second fruit in the noble Dharma.

With the weapons of yoga— arrows of impurity— he shattered the bow of greed, the arrow of conceptual construction, and that great enemy, passion, which had been reduced to its last remnants, by means of his realizations regarding the true nature of the body.
He struck down his enemy— whose weapon was hatred, whose scattered arrows were anger, and whose internal offspring was malice—
with shafts of loving-kindness stored in the quiver of fortitude, released from the bowstring of patience.
Then the Hero severed the three roots of unwholesomeness with the three bases of liberation,
just as one standing at the head of an army might strike down three bow-wielding enemies with three iron-tipped arrows.
Having overcome those who held him back as he sought to transcend the realm of desire,
and having attained the fruit of the non-returner through yoga, he stood like a gateway to the city of Nirvāṇa.

Then he attained the first dhyāna, which is secluded from sensual desires and from defiled states, accompanied by applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), and endowed with the joy and happiness born of seclusion.
Released from the burning fire of desire, he attained supreme joy from the bliss of meditation;
like one weary of the world plunging into water, or a pauper obtaining vast wealth.

There too, having recognized that the discursive thoughts directed toward those qualities and the reflections spread toward their merits and defects were unpeaceful and agitated the mind, he resolved to be free from them.
Just as waves cause agitation in a river carrying deep and clear water,
so too do discursive thoughts, acting like waves, cause agitation in the water of the mind when it has become one-pointed.
Just as sounds cause distress to one who is weary, asleep, or at ease,
so do discursive thoughts become a source of affliction for one who has attained internal one-pointedness.

Then, through the one-pointed state of his mind, he meditated upon that second dhyāna— tranquil within, born of concentration, characterized by joy and bliss, and devoid of both applied and sustained thought— as it arose in succession.
Having attained that meditative absorption, he achieved mental silence and experienced a supreme joy never before obtained;
yet, even in that state of joy, he perceived its defects in the very same way as he had done regarding discursive thoughts.
For wherever one has supreme delight in an object, there indeed arises suffering through its reversal;
therefore, having observed the defects in that delight, he applied himself to the yoga for the cessation of delight.
Then, through detachment from joy, experiencing with the body that bliss which is cherished by the noble ones,
mindful and clearly conscious, the steadfast one dwelt having attained the third dhyāna, remaining equanimous.
Because there is no happiness beyond that, and because there is no further progression of happiness than that,
he who knows the high and the low spoke of the stage of the Śubhakṛtsnas as "supreme" out of loving-kindness.
Even there, in that meditative absorption, he perceived a fault; he considered it to be merely supreme peace and immobility.
For his mind, having set out toward bliss, was still stirred by effortful application.
Wherever there is agitation, there is vibration; and wherever there is vibration, there is suffering.
Therefore, because it is characterized by agitation, those ascetics who desire peace abandon that so-called pleasure.
Then, through the prior abandonment of pleasure and pain as well as mental fluctuation,
one attains the fourth dhyāna, which is characterized by equanimity and mindfulness, and is utterly pure, being neither painful nor pleasant.
But because in that [fourth dhyāna] there is neither pleasure nor pain, and because knowledge exists therein and acts for its sake,
therefore it is described in the method of the fourth dhyāna as "purity of equanimity and mindfulness."
Relying upon that fourth dhyāna, he then set his mind on attaining arhatship,
just as a king, relying on a powerful and noble ally, desires to conquer unconquered territories.
Then, impelled by his cultivation of wisdom, he completely severed with the sword of insight those five higher fetters,
the supreme bonds, the yokes that lead upward.
With the seven nāgas that are the factors of enlightenment, he likewise crushed the seven latent tendencies of the mind,
just as Time, with its seven planets, destroys the seven continents when their destruction is imminent.

For Nanda applied to the faults that same mode of action which belongs to fire, trees, clarified butter, and water toward a headless trunk, wind, fire, and the sun— by means of extinguishing, uprooting, burning, and drying.

Thus, by means of a raft possessing eight qualities, he crossed over the difficult-to-traverse ocean of suffering— characterized by three currents, three crocodiles, three whirlpools, a single body of water, five speeds, two shores, and two sharks.
Having attained arhatship, he was worthy of honor; free from longing, devoid of affection, and without hope;
fearless, undismayed, free from intoxication, and dispassionate, he appeared as if he were someone else through his steadfastness.
Through that instruction of his brother and teacher, and by his own prowess, Nanda—his mind now tranquil and his task accomplished—spoke these words to himself: *Saundarananda 17.62*
Homage be to that Sugata, who, desiring my welfare and possessing a compassionate nature,
has averted many sufferings for me and brought about abundant happiness.
For I, being dragged along the path consisting of suffering by ignoble passion,
have been turned back by the goad of his words, like a rutting elephant by a hook.

"By the command of that compassionate Teacher, having indeed extracted the thorn of passion from my heart, I already experience such great happiness this very day; how much more so when all [defilements] are exhausted and I am fully liberated! (Saundarananda 17.65)
For, having extinguished the blazing fire of desire with the water of fortitude as one might quench a fire with water,
I have now attained supreme joy, like one who has descended into a cool pool during the heat.
Nothing is dear to me, nor is anything undear to me; I have no attachment, so how could there be aversion?
Because of the absence of both, I am immediately happy, like one who has been released from cold and heat.
As one who has found safety from great danger, as one released from a great confinement,
as one without a boat who has reached the further shore of the great ocean, and as one who has emerged from terrifying darkness into light.

Just as health from disease, freedom from debt from an unbearable burden, escape from the presence of an enemy, and abundance from the onset of famine— [all these being] of infinite number— [so too is the attainment of liberation].
In the same way, I have attained supreme peace through the power of that Vināyaka; once again, I offer repeated salutations to him, the Arhat, the Tathāgata. Saundarananda 17.70.
By him I was led to the golden-peaked mountain and shown heaven through the example of the female monkeys;
though my soul was full of desire and I was immersed in this age of Kali consisting of young women, I was drawn out by the celestial damsels who move in the third heaven.

Therefore, having been drawn out from that mire of misfortune by one intent on [his] ruin— like an elephant with loosened limbs from the mud— you are liberated in this ultimate, stainless, passionless, fever-free, sorrowless, and darkness-free True Dharma.
I bow my head to that Great Seer, the supremely compassionate one, who knows the nature of qualities and knows the intentions [of beings];
to the Perfectly Awakened One, possessed of the ten powers, the foremost of physicians, the protector—I bow to him once again. (Saundarananda 17.73)
The seventeenth canto, titled "The Attainment of the Deathless," in the epic poem *Saundarananda*, is concluded.
Canto Eighteen: The Prophecy of His Mission.

Then Nanda, having accomplished his purpose, approached his teacher like a twice-born who has mastered the Vedas as a youth, like a merchant who has swiftly gained a great profit, or like a warrior who has conquered an enemy host.

For at the time of the completion of his knowledge, it is pleasant for the disciple to see the teacher and for the teacher to see the disciple; since he desired to see the Sage, [the king thought], "Your exertion toward me has borne fruit. (Saundarananda 18.2)
For he by whom a distinction has been attained deserves to offer the highest honor to him [who taught it];
how much more so the Noble One who, though still possessing passion, has destroyed pride through a sense of gratitude—let alone one who is free from passion? (Saundarananda 18.3)
For one whose devotion arises from wealth and desire, that devotion remains with its roots firmly established;
but for one whose passionate devotion follows the path of Dharma, his grace penetrates deep into the heart.
Clad in saffron robes and radiant as gold, he then bowed his head to the Guru,
like a *karṇikāra* tree with the copper-red glow of its new leaves stirred by the wind and the brilliant beauty of its blossoms.

Then, for the purpose of demonstrating his own qualities as a disciple, the qualities of the Great Sage as a teacher, and [the excellence of the teaching], he recounted the accomplishment of his task, not out of pride. (Saundarananda 18.6)

O Lord, that extremely sharp thorn of views which had pierced deep into my heart and tormented me intensely has been extracted by the pincers of your words, like a dart removed by one skilled in extracting darts.
I have reached a state free from doubt, for that uncertainty of mine has been severed;
through your teaching, I have come to the true path, like one who had lost his way finding a good guide.

That poison of Kandarpa which I had drunk out of pride with my senses under the sway of desire has been destroyed by the medicine of your words, just as a deadly poison is neutralized by a great antidote.
Birth has come to an end; O you who have cast off birth, I have dwelt perfectly in the practice of the true Dharma.
Everything that was to be done has been accomplished by me; O you whose task is finished, I am one who has become a being among the worlds, yet I am not subject to worldly dharmas.

O Supreme One, like a calf parched with thirst, I have been well-satiated by drinking from your cow: she whose udders are loving-kindness, whose beautiful dewlap is the secondary marks, who yields the milk of the True Dharma, and whose horns are eloquence. (Saundarananda 18.11)
O Sage, understand from me in brief this realization which has come to me as I see;
O Omniscient One, although this is surely known to you, I wish to explain it according to my own manner of expression. (Saundarananda 18.12)
For other virtuous people who desire liberation, having heard the method for liberation from another,
strive happily by that very same path— just as those afflicted by disease do after hearing of one who has been freed from disease.
In this birth, I do not perceive the earth and so forth as the sacrificial altar, nor do I perceive myself as anything within those elements such as the earth;
therefore, I have no attachment to them, and my mind is equal toward both [the internal] and the external body.
Since I perceive the five aggregates, beginning with form, as flickering and devoid of essence,
as well as being selfless and murderous, I am therefore liberated from these inauspicious things.
Since I perceive the arising and passing away of the sense-faculties in all their states,
therefore I have no attachment even toward them, for they are impermanent, selfless, and suffering.

Since I see the world as established in rebirth, entirely essence-less and non-existent, therefore my mind is bound by my intellect; there is no longer any agitation in me by which [I might be moved]. (Saundarananda 18.17)
Since I am unattached to the fourfold variety of food,
being neither infatuated nor bound by it, I am therefore liberated from those three states of existence.
Since my mind is unattached and undetermined toward the phenomena of worldly convention— such as what is seen and heard—
and since it has become equalized therein, I have therefore attained dissociation and am liberated.
Having spoken thus, out of deep reverence for his teacher, he prostrated himself upon the earth with his entire body;
anointed with red sandalwood, he shone like a great golden pillar set upright.

Then, having heard of his former steadfastness and his prophetic declaration, as well as his faith that followed from his adherence to the Dharma, the Sage, whose voice was like the sound of a thundercloud, addressed him who had previously strayed through negligence: *Saundarananda 18.21*
"Arise, you who stand firm in the Dharma cherished by disciples! Why have you fallen at my feet with your head?
To me, a prostration is not such a mark of honor as this very practice of the Dharma. (Saundarananda 18.22)
Today you have truly gone forth as a renunciant, O self-conqueror, by whom sovereignty over the self has been attained;
for the life of a renunciant is excellent for one who has conquered the self, but not for one of fickle mind whose senses remain unsubdued.
Today you are endowed with supreme purity, for your speech, body, and mind are pure;
yet, O gentle one, you shall once again behold the bed of the womb, which is unclean and unpleasant.
Having now understood the Dharma in accordance with that which was heard, just as the hearing of it was purposeful,
one who has completed his studies yet acts contrary to it is indeed censurable, like a man without vigor who has taken up a weapon.
"Oh, how steadfast is your resolve, you whose nature is beyond the sensory realm, that you have set your mind upon the method of liberation!
For it is only the fool who, out of fear of the exhaustion of birth, thinks, 'I shall go to my final end'."
By good fortune, this rare convergence of conditions, so difficult to attain, has not been rendered fruitless by the power of delusion;
for once one has fallen into the depths, one rises up with great difficulty, like a turtle in the ocean encountering the opening of a yoke.

Having conquered Māra, who is difficult to restrain in battle, you are today the hero at the head of combat in this world. For even one who is a hero should be known as no hero at all if he is struck down by faults, just as if by enemies.
Having extinguished the fierce fire of passion today, by good fortune you shall sleep happily, free from burning;
for one whose mind is consumed by the fire of the afflictions (*kleśa*) sleeps in misery, even upon a magnificent bed.
Formerly you were exalted by the intoxication of wealth, but today you are truly prosperous through the cessation of craving.
For as long as a person in this world possesses craving, they are always poor, even if they are fully endowed with riches.
"It is now appropriate for you to declare, 'King Śuddhodana is my father';
yet for one fallen from the Dharma through the downfall brought about by his own fathers, a claim to noble lineage is indeed not to be praised."
By good fortune you have attained supreme peace, like one who has reached the heart of the matter after crossing a wilderness;
for everyone caught in the cycle of existence is afflicted by fear, just as one who has entered a wilderness.
"When shall I see Nanda, living in the forest, subsisting on alms, humble, and composed?"—such was my desire to behold you in the past; thus it is by good fortune that you are now visible to me.
For even one who is formless may be beautiful when well-adorned with his own most excellent virtues; yet one who is encompassed by defiling faults is truly ugly, even if he be handsome to behold.
Today your wisdom has reached its highest excellence, for by it you have accomplished your entire purpose.
For even one exalted by learning lacks true wisdom if his intellect does not arise toward the supreme good. (Saundarananda 18.35)
Even among people with eyes wide open, the eye of one who lacks the eye consisting of wisdom is as if closed; for even though he possesses physical sight, he has no true vision.

Afflicted by the need to counteract suffering, the world undergoes exhaustion through agriculture and other such labors; yet that suffering returns incessantly and even increases—until today its end has been brought about by you through wisdom.

"The world constantly exerts itself, thinking, 'May there be no suffering for me; may there be only happiness for me. Yet it does not know how that [happiness] might truly come to pass, as it has now been attained by you in its proper way, so difficult to obtain. (Saundarananda 18.38)

When the Tathāgata had spoken these and other words for his benefit, Nanda—his intellect and mind thus made firm, and indifferent to both praise and blame—spoke these words with palms joined in reverence: *Saundarananda 18.39*
Oh, how you, who perceive the subtle distinctions, have shown me this special compassion!
For, O Blessed One, though I was without desire, I have been rescued from the mud of passion and from the fear of saṃsāra.
If I had not been rescued by you, my brother and guide to the highest good, as well as by my father established in the fruit [of liberation] and likewise by my mother,
I would have perished like one who has strayed from his caravan, having failed to achieve his purpose.
For one who is peaceful and contented, solitude is happiness; for the investigator who has realized reality, it is happiness;
and for one whose pride is abandoned and who is free from intoxication, detachment is happiness for one whose mind is unattached.

For now that I have thoroughly understood reality, completely shaken off my faults, and attained peace, I am intent only upon my own hermitage; I think of neither those people, nor the apsarases, nor the gods.
For having tasted this pure happiness born of tranquility, my mind no longer longs for pleasure born of desire;
it is like a celestial being who, having consumed nectar, has no further craving for even the most costly food not brought by the gods.
Alas! The world, its vision obscured by blind ignorance, does not perceive the supreme bliss within the inner cloth;
for, having cast aside the firm and middle self-bliss, it instead pursues the toil for the sake of sensual pleasure.

For just as a fool, having come to a mine of jewels, might discard the jewels and carry away worthless stones, so too one might cast aside the supreme bliss of perfect enlightenment and labor instead for the sake of attaining the pleasures of the senses. (Saundarananda 18.46)
Oh, how supreme is the Tathāgata’s desire to favor sentient beings, his mind overflowing with extreme loving-kindness!
For, O Sage, casting aside the highest bliss of meditative absorption, you exert yourself for the sake of ending the suffering of others.
How indeed can I possibly repay you today, my teacher, who desires my welfare and is compassionate toward me—
you by whom I have been rescued from the ocean of existence, like one whose ship was shattered by the waves of the great sea?

Then the minister, having heard his reasoned speech which indicated that all taints were abandoned, spoke these words, which only one who is a mass of glory—the unsurpassed among speakers—is worthy to utter: Saundarananda 18.49.
O wise one, you alone, having accomplished your purpose and knowing the ultimate truth, ought to speak this;
like a great merchant who has crossed the wilderness and attained his goal, you have fulfilled the task for your excellent guide.

Just as an accomplished arhat whose mind is fully stilled perceives the Buddha, the charioteer who tames men, so too does one who has seen the truth; but how much less can an ordinary person, even if possessed of intelligence, comprehend him in such a way? (Saundarananda 18.51)
This gratitude of yours is truly worthy of you, whose mind is completely liberated from passion and ignorance;
for in a world established in the preponderance of passion, O grateful one, the state of being grateful is indeed rare to find.

Since you possess the true Dharma and its logical sequence, and since you have both faith in me and skill in spiritual attainment, I have much more that I wish to say to you; for as one who is humble and devoted, you deserve to receive my instruction.
"You have accomplished your task and attained the supreme goal; there is not even the slightest thing remaining for you to do.
Therefore, O gentle one, from this point forward, move through the world out of compassion, liberating others who have fallen into distress. (Saundarananda 18.54)
For this very purpose, the base man undertakes action; the mediocre man, however, undertakes action pertaining to both worlds;
the middling man undertakes action for the sake of fruit in the world beyond alone; but the one of distinguished dharma acts again for the sake of non-activity.

Among these, he is considered even more excellent than the most excellent who, having attained the supreme and ultimate Dharma, disregards his own personal exertion and desires to teach tranquility to others as well. (Saundarananda 18.56)
Therefore, O steadfast one, setting aside your own task here, you should now perform the task of others as well;
while beings wander with their minds shrouded in darkness, let this lamp of sacred learning be held aloft in the night.
Let the astonished people in the city say, while you remain there delivering teachings on the Dharma:
"Oh, how wonderful! Even this one who is still possessed by passion delivers such discourse for the sake of liberation! (Saundarananda 18.58)
For having heard your firm resolve, her mind will surely turn away from various worldly desires;
following your example at home, that wife of yours will also make stories of dispassion toward women the talk among women.
When you have become firmly established in supreme steadfastness and have realized the true nature of reality, she will certainly no longer find delight in the household life—
just as the discerning mind finds no pleasure in sensual pleasures when it is secluded and characterized by tranquility and self-restraint.
Thus, having bowed his head and simultaneously grasped both the words and the feet of the Arhat, the Teacher of supreme compassion,
he departed from the side of the Sage— composed, with a tranquil heart, his task accomplished, and free from pride like an elephant.
At the proper time, he entered the city for alms, captivating the eyes of the people;
equal toward gain and loss, pleasure and pain, and other such things, his senses composed and free from desire,
he delivered a discourse on liberation to those who sought it at that moment.
Neither disparaging others who have gone astray, nor exalting oneself.
Thus, this work, which contains the essence of liberation for the sake of tranquility rather than mere pleasure,
has been composed by means of the artifice of poetry in order to capture the attention of those whose minds are otherwise occupied;
for whatever else has been composed here by me besides liberation, that is due to the nature of poetry.
"How might this be made pleasant to drink, like bitter medicine mixed with honey? // Saund_18.63 //
Having observed that the world for the most part is intent on the pleasures of the senses and averse to liberation,

I have here related the truth under the guise of poetry, [stating] that liberation is supreme. Having understood this, one should attentively grasp from it that which pertains to tranquility, and not the mere artistic embellishment.
From dust born of the elements, gold as a precious substance is inevitably produced. // Saund 18.64 //
The eighteenth canto, titled "The Declaration of Knowledge," in the epic poem *Saundarananda*, is completed.
